questions.stem: Airway edema is confined to the subglottic region at the cricoid ring; the trachea below it is normal on CT. How is the obstructed level classified?
options: Upper airway, because it is above the trachea
Lower airway, because it is below the vocal cords
Lower airway, because the cricoid is the first tracheal ring
Neither division; it is a transition zone
questions.explanation: The upper airway runs from the nose and mouth through the pharynx, larynx, and cricoid cartilage; the lower airway begins at the trachea. The tempting error is calling anything below the cords 'lower airway.' The subglottic cricoid ring still belongs to the upper airway, which also matters clinically because it is a fixed, complete ring that cannot expand around edema.

questions.stem: A mass compresses the distal trachea just above the carina, and the patient obstructs after induction. Why would an emergency cricothyrotomy fail to relieve the obstruction?
options: The cricothyroid membrane sits at the level of the carina
The lesion lies distal to the cricothyroid membrane
A surgical airway cannot deliver positive pressure
Distal tracheal lesions obstruct only during spontaneous breathing
questions.explanation: A cricothyrotomy enters the airway between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, so it bypasses upper-airway obstruction only. A distal tracheal mass is a lower-airway problem below that entry point. The last option reverses the real concern: extrathoracic and intrathoracic masses often worsen when spontaneous ventilation and muscle tone are lost, not only during spontaneous breathing.

questions.stem: A neonate has micrognathia, cleft palate, and a posteriorly displaced tongue. Maldevelopment of which pharyngeal arch best explains these findings, and what airway problem results?
options: First arch; subglottic narrowing at the cricoid
First arch; the tongue obstructs the oropharynx
Sixth arch; bilateral vocal cord paralysis

The fourth and sixth arches contribute laryngeal cartilages and muscles, so their defects produce laryngeal problems rather than the mandibular pattern described here.

questions.stem: A patient with a new tracheostomy breathes room air through the stoma. Which THREE nasal functions are now bypassed? (Select 3)
options: Protection of the lower airway from aspiration
questions.explanation: The nose humidifies and filters inspired gas and adds resistance to airflow; a tracheostomy routes gas below all three. Loss of humidification is why tracheostomy secretions thicken and why humidified gas or a heat-moisture exchanger is used. Phonation, aspiration protection, and cough are laryngeal functions, so they belong to a different structure even though a tracheostomy can affect them.

questions.stem: During awake nasal fiberoptic intubation, the anterior nares were well topicalized, but the patient has sharp pain as the scope passes the posterior nasal septum. Which sensory distribution was inadequately anesthetized?
options: Ophthalmic branch (V1) via the anterior ethmoidal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the pharyngeal plexus
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Maxillary branch (V2) via the sphenopalatine ganglion
questions.explanation: Nasal sensation comes from the trigeminal nerve, with V1 covering the anterior septum and lateral wall through the anterior ethmoidal nerve and V2 covering the posterior two-thirds through branches of the sphenopalatine ganglion. Pain only at the posterior septum points to V2. The glossopharyngeal nerve takes over in the oropharynx, which the scope has not reached yet.

questions.stem: Brisk posterior epistaxis begins during nasotracheal intubation. Which arterial source most likely supplies this bleeding?
options: Sphenopalatine branch of the maxillary artery
Anterior ethmoidal branch of the ophthalmic artery
Superior labial branch of the facial artery
Superior laryngeal branch of the superior thyroid artery
questions.explanation: The nose is supplied by branches of the maxillary, ophthalmic, and facial arteries. Posterior bleeding is usually from the sphenopalatine branch of the maxillary artery, while anterior septal bleeding involves ophthalmic (ethmoidal) and facial (labial) branches. Posterior bleeds are harder to control and can flood the airway, which is one reason a topical vasoconstrictor is applied before nasal instrumentation.

questions.stem: A sedated patient breathing with the mouth closed develops snoring obstruction that resolves as soon as the mouth is opened, before any jaw thrust. Which structure most likely caused the obstruction?
options: Tongue base against the posterior oropharynx
Soft palate against the posterior nasopharynx
Epiglottis folding over the laryngeal inlet
Vocal cords adducting in partial laryngospasm
questions.explanation: Loss of pharyngeal dilator tone lets both the tongue and the soft palate fall posteriorly. With the mouth closed, a collapsed soft palate blocks the nasal route, and opening the mouth gives an oral path around it. Tongue-base obstruction typically needs jaw thrust or an oral airway to relieve it, and laryngospasm would not resolve with simple mouth opening.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old with Pierre Robin sequence has obstructed breathing when supine that improves when placed prone. What explains the improvement?
options: Prone position widens a narrow subglottis
The small mandible is pulled forward by gravity
The tongue falls forward away from the pharynx
questions.explanation: Pierre Robin sequence combines mandibular hypoplasia with glossoptosis, so the tongue falls back into the oropharynx when supine, and prone positioning lets it fall forward. Floppy supraglottic tissue describes laryngomalacia, the subglottis is not the obstructed level, and positioning does not change mandibular size. Down syndrome obstructs through relative macroglossia instead.

questions.stem: After palatal surgery, a patient has nasal regurgitation of liquids when swallowing. Dysfunction of which portion of the palate best explains this?
options: Soft palate, the mobile posterior third
Hard palate, the fixed anterior two-thirds
Soft palate, the fixed anterior third
Hard palate, the mobile posterior third
questions.explanation: The hard palate is the fixed anterior two-thirds, and the soft palate is the mobile posterior third. During swallowing the soft palate elevates to seal off the nasopharynx; if it cannot, liquid escapes into the nose. The distractors swap the position and mobility of the two parts, which is the detail this item tests.

questions.stem: During a preoperative exam, the seated patient protrudes the tongue without phonation; the soft palate, fauces, and full uvula are seen but the tonsillar pillars are not. Which class and meaning fit?
questions.explanation: Mallampati class I shows the pillars along with the soft palate, fauces, and uvula, and losing the pillars while keeping the full uvula is class II, which carries low predicted difficulty. Class III shows only the soft palate and base of the uvula and raises concern. Mallampati is still combined with other predictors.

questions.stem: Without phonation, only the soft palate and base of the uvula are visible. When the patient says 'ah,' the fauces and full uvula come into view. What should be documented?
options: Class II, because the best view obtained is recorded
Class I, because phonation reveals the fauces
Class IV, because the uvula is initially hidden
Class III, because the exam is graded without phonation
questions.explanation: Mallampati is assessed sitting, mouth open, tongue protruded, without phonation. Phonation elevates the soft palate and artificially improves the view, so grading the phonated view underestimates difficulty. The unphonated view of soft palate plus uvula base is class III; class IV would show only the hard palate.

questions.stem: During deep general anesthesia, regurgitated gastric contents reach the pharynx. Which mechanism best explains failure of the barrier at the top of the esophagus?
options: Volatile agents increase lower esophageal sphincter tone
Anesthetics reduce upper esophageal sphincter tone
The epiglottis no longer seals the esophageal inlet
Relaxed vocal cords open the esophageal inlet
questions.explanation: The upper esophageal sphincter is the main barrier between the esophagus and pharynx, and anesthetic agents relax it. The epiglottis protects the laryngeal inlet, not the esophagus, and the vocal cords guard the trachea. Volatile agents reduce rather than increase sphincter tone, so the second option has the direction backward.

questions.stem: During awake oral fiberoptic intubation, glossopharyngeal blocks are effective, yet touching the epiglottis still triggers coughing. Which nerve was most likely missed?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Lingual branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The internal superior laryngeal nerve carries sensation from the epiglottis down to the vocal cords and needs its own block or topicalization. The external branch is motor to the cricothyroid, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve carries sensation below the cords. Because the glossopharyngeal block already worked, its lingual branch is not the gap.

questions.stem: After complete transection of one recurrent laryngeal nerve, which intrinsic laryngeal muscle on that side still functions?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor, is lost with RLN injury, which is why the affected cord cannot open.

questions.stem: After thyroidectomy, a singer cannot reach high notes and her voice fatigues, but laryngoscopy shows normal abduction and adduction. Which injury fits best?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid lengthens and tenses the cords and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, so injury reduces pitch range while cord movement stays normal. The internal branch is sensory, so its injury causes aspiration risk rather than pitch loss. RLN injuries change cord movement, which this laryngoscopy rules out.

questions.stem: After thyroidectomy, a patient has a breathy, hoarse voice and coughs with thin liquids, but no stridor. Which nerve injury best fits?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: Unilateral RLN injury leaves one cord unable to close fully, producing a breathy, hoarse voice and aspiration, while the opposite cord keeps the airway open. Bilateral injury leaves both cords near midline with stridor. Internal SLN injury causes aspiration without hoarseness, and external SLN injury affects pitch without a breathy voice.

questions.stem: Minutes after thyroidectomy extubation, severe inspiratory stridor develops. Both vocal cords are fixed near midline, and CPAP with jaw thrust does not improve air entry. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue CPAP with Larson maneuver pressure
questions.explanation: Bilateral RLN injury leaves both cords near midline, and the obstruction is mechanical and persistent, so the airway must be secured. Laryngospasm usually breaks with CPAP, jaw thrust, or a small dose of succinylcholine; failure of those measures with fixed cords points away from spasm. Racemic epinephrine treats edema, which would not fix immobile cords.

questions.stem: For awake oral fiberoptic intubation, which THREE techniques together cover sensation from the tongue base to the trachea? (Select 3)
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve block in the tracheoesophageal groove
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves supply the pharynx and larynx. The glossopharyngeal block covers the posterior tongue and pharynx, the SLN block covers epiglottis to cords, and transtracheal lidocaine covers the cords and trachea, which receive RLN sensory fibers. The hypoglossal nerve is motor, the sphenopalatine block serves the nasal route, and a direct RLN block would paralyze the cords.

questions.stem: After a traumatic intubation, a patient is persistently hoarse and CT shows a dislocated paired cartilage on which the vocal cord inserts. Which cartilage is injured?
questions.explanation: The vocal cord attaches posteriorly to the vocal process of the arytenoid, a paired cartilage that pivots on the cricoid, so dislocation causes hoarseness and a weak voice. The corniculate and cuneiform cartilages are also paired but are small and do not anchor the cords, and the cricoid is unpaired, like the thyroid and epiglottis.

questions.stem: After a traumatic intubation, a patient is hoarse; laryngoscopy shows one immobile cord with its posterior attachment displaced, and laryngeal EMG shows normal nerve function. Which management is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: An immobile cord with a displaced posterior attachment and normal laryngeal EMG points to arytenoid dislocation rather than nerve paralysis, and early closed reduction gives the best chance of restoring function before fibrosis fixes the joint. Long observation allows ankylosis, medialization treats permanent paralysis, and steroids alone do not relocate the cartilage.

questions.stem: Which THREE functions are performed primarily by the larynx? (Select 3)
options: Protection of the lower airway from aspiration
questions.explanation: The larynx protects the lower airway, drives gag and cough reflexes, produces voice, and maintains patency. Humidification, filtration, and added resistance are nasal functions. Pairing these with laryngeal functions tests whether the two upper-airway regions are kept distinct.

questions.stem: In a cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate emergency, a clinician palpates the membrane immediately above the thyroid cartilage and incises it. Which structure has been entered?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, below the thyroid cartilage. A membrane above the thyroid cartilage is the thyrohyoid membrane, which lies at or above the cords and is the wrong entry site. The cricotracheal ligament and tracheal interspaces are lower still.

questions.stem: In an obese neck, the thyroid notch cannot be felt, but a firm complete ring is palpated low in the neck. Where should the cricothyroid membrane be sought relative to that ring?
options: At the level of the hyoid
questions.explanation: The firm complete ring is the cricoid, and the cricothyroid membrane sits just above it, between it and the thyroid cartilage. Working upward from the cricoid is useful when the thyroid notch is hard to feel. Moving below the cricoid would place the incision in the trachea.

questions.stem: Bleeding arises from the supraglottic larynx. Which arterial pathway supplies this region?
options: Inferior thyroid to inferior laryngeal artery
Superior thyroid to inferior laryngeal artery
Superior thyroid to superior laryngeal artery
Inferior thyroid to superior laryngeal artery
questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal artery arises from the superior thyroid artery and supplies the supraglottic larynx. The inferior laryngeal artery arises from the inferior thyroid artery and supplies the infraglottic larynx. The crossed pairings test whether both the parent vessel and the branch are known.

questions.stem: A subglottic biopsy site continues to bleed. Ligation of which parent trunk would reduce flow to this region?
questions.explanation: The infraglottic larynx is supplied by the inferior laryngeal artery, a branch of the inferior thyroid artery. The superior thyroid artery supplies the supraglottic larynx through the superior laryngeal artery. The lingual and facial arteries supply the tongue and face.

questions.stem: After extubation in stage II, a patient has silent chest-wall effort with no airflow. Contraction of which muscle group produces this closure?
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is reflex contraction of the intrinsic adductors, such as the lateral cricoarytenoid and thyroarytenoid, which close the glottis tightly. The posterior cricoarytenoid abducts and would open the cords, extrinsic muscles move the whole larynx, and the pharyngeal constrictors act during swallowing rather than glottic closure.

questions.stem: After a neck dissection, a patient aspirates because the larynx does not elevate during swallowing, yet the cords open and close normally. Which muscle group is impaired?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic laryngeal muscles position and elevate the larynx during breathing, phonation, and swallowing. Normal cord movement shows the intrinsic muscles are working. Constrictors propel the bolus but do not lift the larynx, and the muscles of mastication act on the jaw.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy with a Miller blade, the tip is placed in the vallecula and the epiglottis keeps falling over the glottis. What correction is needed?
options: Pass the tip beneath the epiglottis and lift it
Seat the tip deeper in the vallecula and lift
Apply BURP to bring the cords into view
Lever the handle back toward the upper teeth
questions.explanation: A straight Miller blade is designed to pass beneath the epiglottis and lift it directly, which is useful when the epiglottis is long or floppy. Seating it deeper in the vallecula uses the Macintosh mechanism and may still fail with a straight blade, BURP moves the larynx but not the epiglottis, and levering risks dental injury.

questions.stem: With a Macintosh blade in the vallecula, lifting does not raise the epiglottis and the glottis remains hidden. What is the most likely technical cause?
options: The tip is beneath the epiglottis instead of in the vallecula
The tip is not seated deep enough to tension the hyoepiglottic ligament
The blade tip is in the piriform sinus instead of midline
The blade is lifting directly on the posterior pharyngeal wall
questions.explanation: A Macintosh blade works indirectly: the tip must press into the base of the vallecula to tension the hyoepiglottic ligament, which raises the epiglottis. If the tip is too shallow, the ligament stays slack and the epiglottis does not move. A tip beneath the epiglottis would lift it directly, which would improve the view, not prevent it.

questions.stem: A chest radiograph shows the ETT tip at the level of the cricoid cartilage, just below the vocal cords. What is the main concern?
options: The tube is ideally placed in the upper trachea
The tube is too deep and near the carina
Too shallow; the cuff likely sits in the larynx
The tube is likely in the esophagus
questions.explanation: The trachea begins at the cricoid and ends at the carina, and a well-placed tip sits in the mid-trachea several centimeters above the carina. A tip at the cricoid means the cuff is in or near the larynx, risking cord and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and accidental extubation. Tracheal position on film makes esophageal placement unlikely.

questions.stem: An ETT is well positioned with the head neutral. The head is then fully extended for thyroid surgery. What happens to the tube tip?
options: It moves toward the vocal cords
It advances into the right mainstem
It stays fixed since it is taped
questions.explanation: Neck extension withdraws the ETT tip toward the vocal cords, by up to about 2 cm, while flexion advances it toward the carina. Taping at the lip does not prevent movement relative to the trachea, so after extension the cuff may sit at the cords and accidental extubation becomes more likely.

questions.stem: A large-bore orogastric tube or TEE probe compresses the trachea. Which tracheal wall is most vulnerable and why?
options: Anterior wall, because it lacks cartilage
Posterior wall, because it lacks cartilage
Posterior wall, because the cartilage is thinner there
Lateral walls, because the rings are incomplete laterally
questions.explanation: Tracheal rings are C-shaped, open posteriorly, and the posterior wall is the membranous trachealis muscle adjacent to the esophagus. That wall has no cartilage support, so esophageal devices can indent it. The anterior and lateral walls are supported by cartilage.

questions.stem: During RSI, an assistant places pressure on the thyroid cartilage instead of the cricoid. Why is the cricoid the correct target?
options: It sits directly over the lower esophageal sphincter
Its incomplete ring lets the trachea flatten
It is the only mobile laryngeal cartilage
Its complete ring compresses the esophagus
questions.explanation: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway, so backward force passes through it to the esophagus behind it while the airway lumen stays open. The thyroid cartilage is open posteriorly, so pressing it distorts the larynx and worsens the view. The cricoid sits over the upper esophagus, not the lower sphincter.

questions.stem: During a forceful cough, which posterior tracheal structure contracts to narrow the lumen and then relaxes to allow esophageal expansion during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The trachealis spans the open posterior ends of the C-shaped rings. It narrows the lumen to increase airflow velocity during cough and relaxes so the esophagus can expand with a bolus. The cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter, and the posterior cricoarytenoid abducts the vocal cords.

questions.stem: During severe bronchospasm, why do the smallest conducting airways narrow far more than the bronchi?
options: They have more cartilage, which buckles under muscle tension
They lack cartilage, so patency depends on smooth muscle tone
They lack smooth muscle, so they cannot dilate
They are lined by type I pneumocytes that swell

questions.stem: After intubation, a patient has absent left breath sounds with the tube at 27 cm at the lips. Which anatomic feature explains why the tube entered the right mainstem?
options: The right bronchus is narrower than the left
The carina sits to the right of midline
The left bronchus is shorter than the right
The right bronchus leaves at a shallower angle
questions.explanation: The right mainstem leaves the trachea at about 25 to 30 degrees, nearly in line with the trachea, while the left leaves at about 45 to 55 degrees, so a deep tube follows the straighter right path. The right bronchus is also wider and shorter than the left, so the other choices reverse the actual anatomy.

questions.stem: After repositioning, PIP and plateau pressure both rise, SpO2 falls, left breath sounds are absent, BP is unchanged, and the ETT lip mark moved from 22 to 25 cm. What is the most likely problem and response?
options: Right mainstem intubation; withdraw to the prior depth
Left tension pneumothorax; perform needle decompression
Left mainstem intubation; withdraw to the prior depth
Bronchospasm; deepen anesthesia and give albuterol
questions.explanation: Rising PIP and plateau pressure point to reduced compliance, and the deeper lip mark points to tube migration. The right mainstem is shorter, wider, and more vertical, so a deep tube enters it and the left lung goes silent. Pneumothorax is the dangerous look-alike, but stable BP and a changed tube depth favor endobronchial intubation. Bronchospasm raises PIP with little change in plateau.

questions.stem: During one-lung ventilation with a right-sided double-lumen tube, SpO2 falls and bronchoscopy shows the bronchial cuff at the upper-lobe takeoff. Why does this happen readily?
options: The right mainstem is narrower than the left one
The left upper lobe bronchus arises near the carina
The RUL bronchus arises about 2.5 cm from the carina
The right mainstem angle is steeper than the left
questions.explanation: The right upper-lobe bronchus arises only about 2.5 cm below the carina, so a right-sided bronchial cuff easily blocks it and causes hypoxemia, which is why left-sided tubes are usually preferred. The right mainstem is wider and straighter than the left, and the left mainstem is longer before it divides.

questions.stem: Airway instrumentation under light anesthesia triggers reflex bronchoconstriction. Which efferent pathway mediates it, and which drug class blocks that limb?
options: Phrenic efferents; blocked by neuromuscular blockers
Glossopharyngeal efferents; blocked by local anesthetics
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the trachea and bronchi, and acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors causes bronchoconstriction. Anticholinergics block that efferent limb. Beta-agonists relax smooth muscle but do not block the reflex pathway, and the phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm.

questions.stem: After turning a patient prone, the patient bucks with abrupt tachycardia and hypertension under stable anesthetic depth, and the ETT appears deeper at the teeth. What is most likely being stimulated?
questions.explanation: The carina is highly sensitive, and contact causes coughing, bronchospasm, and sympathetic responses. A tube that has migrated deeper during positioning can touch it. The vocal cords and epiglottis lie above the tube tip and are not being newly stimulated by a deeper tube.

questions.stem: An infant born at 30 weeks has surfactant deficiency. In which lung development stage did surfactant production begin, and which stage follows it?
questions.explanation: Lung development runs embryonic, pseudoglandular, canalicular, terminal sac, then alveolar. Vascularization and early surfactant production begin in the canalicular stage, which is followed by the terminal sac stage and then alveolar maturation that continues after birth. The pseudoglandular stage is defined by airway branching rather than surfactant.

questions.stem: By approximately what gestational time are bronchopulmonary segments recognizable?
questions.explanation: Bronchopulmonary segments are recognizable by about day 42. Week 16 marks the end of the pseudoglandular branching phase, week 26 is when the blood-gas barrier begins forming, and week 36 is late saccular development. This item remains a recall question; it is kept because segment anatomy underlies lung isolation and bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: A mother in preterm labor at 28 weeks is expected to deliver within days. Which maternal therapy most directly speeds fetal surfactant production?
questions.explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids such as betamethasone accelerate maturation of type II pneumocytes, which begin producing surfactant in the canalicular stage, and they lower neonatal respiratory distress syndrome when given before about 34 weeks. Magnesium is given for fetal neuroprotection, and indomethacin and terbutaline are tocolytics.

questions.stem: An infant is born at 24 weeks. Which developmental limitation most restricts gas exchange?
options: Airway branching has not yet produced bronchioles
Surfactant production has not yet begun
The alveolar-capillary barrier is still forming
questions.explanation: The blood-gas barrier begins forming around week 26, so an infant born earlier has limited surface for diffusion. Branching to terminal bronchioles is completed in the pseudoglandular stage, and surfactant production has begun (though in small amounts) in the canalicular stage. Alveolar septation continues for years after birth.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old who had significant lung injury as a neonate shows continued improvement in gas exchange. Which developmental process best explains this?
options: New conducting airways form throughout childhood
Surfactant production begins only after birth
Alveoli keep forming until about age 3 and beyond
questions.explanation: Alveolar development continues until about 3 years of age and beyond with growth, so new gas-exchange units can still form. Airway branching is complete well before birth, and surfactant production starts in the canalicular stage.

questions.stem: A fetus is exposed at 12 weeks' gestation to a drug that disrupts lung development. Which process is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Week 12 falls in the pseudoglandular stage (weeks 6 to 16), which is defined by rapid branching of the airways to the terminal bronchioles. Surfactant production begins in the canalicular stage, the blood-gas barrier forms around week 26, and alveolar septation occurs late and continues after birth.

questions.stem: A neonate has a left posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Failure of which embryologic structure most likely explains the defect?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal folds, dorsal esophageal mesentery, and body wall. Posterolateral defects come from failed closure of the pleuroperitoneal folds. The septum transversum forms the central tendon, so it is the tempting but incorrect choice for a posterolateral defect.

questions.stem: A newborn has severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest. Which developmental defect best explains the physiology?
questions.explanation: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia permits abdominal viscera to enter the thorax, compressing the developing lung and causing pulmonary hypoplasia. Bowel sounds in the chest with a scaphoid abdomen strongly point to this defect.

questions.stem: A neonate with esophageal atresia also has a tracheoesophageal fistula. Abnormal separation of which embryologic structure explains the defect?
options: Neural crest of the pharyngeal arches
Foregut endoderm dividing into two tubes
questions.explanation: The epithelium of the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli develops from foregut endoderm, which normally separates into the trachea and esophagus, and incomplete separation causes a tracheoesophageal fistula. Supporting cartilage and muscle come from mesoderm, the septum transversum forms part of the diaphragm, and neural crest forms facial and arch structures.

questions.stem: A neonate with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia has pulmonary hypoplasia with abnormal pulmonary vessels. Disrupted signaling of which growth-factor pair contributes?
questions.explanation: Fibroblast growth factor 10 from the mesenchyme drives branching of the airway buds, and vascular endothelial growth factor drives pulmonary vascular development, so disrupted signaling contributes to the hypoplastic lungs and abnormal vessels seen in CDH. EGF, IGF-1, TGF-beta, and PDGF have other growth roles, and erythropoietin and GM-CSF act on blood cells.

questions.stem: During swallowing, which structure most directly deflects material away from the glottic opening?
questions.explanation: During swallowing, the larynx rises and the epiglottis tilts backward over the laryngeal inlet, deflecting food toward the piriform recesses and esophagus. The soft palate seals the nasopharynx, the aryepiglottic folds border the inlet, and the upper esophageal sphincter opens to receive the bolus rather than deflecting it.

questions.stem: During awake flexible laryngoscopy, the scope tip drifts lateral to the fold that runs from the epiglottis to the arytenoid. Where is the tip now?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral borders of the laryngeal inlet, and the piriform recesses lie just lateral to them, which is where a scope drifts and where fish bones often lodge. The vallecula sits between the tongue base and epiglottis, and the ventricle and vestibular folds lie inside the larynx below the inlet.

questions.stem: A fish bone lodged in the piriform recess causes numbness of the ipsilateral supraglottic mucosa. Which nerve runs just beneath the recess mucosa?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs beneath the mucosa of the piriform recess, which is why foreign bodies there can cause supraglottic numbness and why topical anesthesia applied there blocks the nerve. The external branch is motor to the cricothyroid, the recurrent laryngeal nerve lies below the cords, and the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the oropharynx.

questions.stem: During thyroid lobectomy, the surgeon ligates vessels at the superior pole of the gland. Which nerve is at greatest risk at that site?
questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery near the upper pole, so it is at risk during superior pole ligation, and injury weakens the cricothyroid and pitch control. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is near the inferior thyroid artery, the internal branch enters through the thyrohyoid membrane, and the hypoglossal nerve lies higher.

questions.stem: After total thyroidectomy with bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, the patient has stridor and the cords sit near midline. Loss of which muscle explains the obstruction?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the vocal cords, so bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves the cords near midline with stridor and obstruction that may need reintubation or tracheostomy. The thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid adduct the cords, and the cricothyroid is supplied by the external superior laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: During laryngospasm, which intrinsic muscles are most responsible for forceful vocal-cord adduction?
questions.explanation: The thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid, both supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, adduct the cords and close the glottis in laryngospasm. The cricothyroid, supplied by the external superior laryngeal nerve, tenses the cords rather than closing them, and the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor, so it opposes laryngospasm.

questions.stem: A patient has limited mouth opening and a short neck before thyroidectomy. What is the main purpose of the airway assessment?
options: Choose one technique and commit to it
Find challenges and build a backup plan
Decide whether to avoid general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Airway assessment identifies likely challenges, such as limited mouth opening or a short neck, so a patient-specific primary plan and backups can be prepared. No exam predicts difficulty with certainty, committing to one technique leaves no fallback, and avoiding general anesthesia is only one possible result of the assessment.

questions.stem: Mallampati is I, but thyromental distance is 4 cm and neck extension is limited. Which interpretation is best?
options: Trust Mallampati, the most reliable test
Combine predictors, as no test is reliable
questions.explanation: Individual airway tests have low sensitivity and specificity, so findings are combined. A short thyromental distance and limited neck extension raise concern despite Mallampati class I and justify preparing for a difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Which four components of airway management should be assessed before anesthesia? (Select 4)
options: Direct or video laryngoscopy with intubation
questions.explanation: Airway planning considers each technique separately: bag-mask ventilation, laryngoscopy and intubation, supraglottic airway placement, and emergency front-of-neck access, since failure of one does not predict failure of all. Mallampati class and neck circumference are single predictors that feed into these assessments rather than being techniques themselves.

questions.stem: Which two historical clues should raise the strongest concern for prior airway difficulty? (Select 2)
options: Postoperative nausea after a prior case
A prior anesthetic lasting over 6 hours
questions.explanation: Chipped teeth after a prior anesthetic and an unexpected ICU admission suggest the previous airway was difficult, as do severe sore throat or being told intubation was hard. Prior PONV, a long case, or uneventful LMA or spinal anesthetics do not point to airway difficulty.

questions.stem: A department performs 5,000 tracheal intubations each year. If difficult intubation occurs in about 1.5 to 8.5% of cases, how many difficult intubations are expected?
questions.explanation: Applying an incidence of about 1.5 to 8.5% to 5,000 intubations gives roughly 75 to 425 difficult intubations per year, varying with the population and setting. This frequency is why difficult-airway equipment and algorithms must be immediately available.

questions.stem: The original Mallampati scale had three classes. Which class did the Samsoon and Young modification add?
questions.explanation: Samsoon and Young added class IV, in which only the hard palate is visible, to the original three-class Mallampati scale. Class 0, a visible epiglottis tip, was described later, and classes I and III were part of the original scale. Classes III and IV are associated with difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Before surgery, a patient is examined supine with the tongue inside the mouth while saying 'ah,' and the full uvula is seen. Why is the recorded Mallampati class unreliable?
options: Do it supine with the head flexed
Do it with the mouth half open
Do it seated, tongue fully protruded
questions.explanation: The Mallampati exam is done with the patient seated, mouth fully open, and tongue maximally protruded, usually without phonation. Supine positioning and phonation change how much of the oropharynx is seen, so the result does not match the validated classes. Sedation before the exam alters tone and cooperation.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati findings of soft palate and uvula base only, with a 7-cm thyromental distance and 4-cm mouth opening. What should be documented?
options: Class II; reassuring with a normal TMD
Class IV; implies a hard palate view
Class III; affects mask ventilation only
questions.explanation: Seeing only the soft palate and base of the uvula is Mallampati class III, which is associated with higher risk of difficult laryngoscopy even when other measurements are normal. Class II would show the full uvula, and class IV shows only the hard palate. Mallampati mainly predicts laryngoscopy, though it also contributes to mask difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient's Mallampati exam shows only the hard palate, but thyromental distance and neck mobility are normal. Which preparation is most appropriate?
options: Blind nasal intubation as the plan
A smaller blade for the large tongue
questions.explanation: Seeing only the hard palate is Mallampati class IV, which raises the risk of difficult laryngoscopy even with other normal findings, so a videolaryngoscope, bougie, and backup devices are prepared. Blind nasal intubation is not a first plan, a smaller blade gives less tongue control, and standard laryngoscopy alone has no backup.

questions.stem: In a preoperative clinic, a patient with normal measurements otherwise shows only the hard palate on Mallampati exam. What does this finding mean?
options: Class IV; difficult DL is more likely
Soft palate and uvula base; DL is easy
Uvula and pillars hidden; mask is easy
Pillars hidden; only mask ventilation is harder
questions.explanation: Seeing only the hard palate is Mallampati class IV, and classes III and IV are associated with a higher likelihood of difficult laryngoscopy because the tongue fills the oral cavity. Soft palate and uvula base describe class III, and class IV raises concern for laryngoscopy as well as mask ventilation.

questions.stem: The epiglottis is visible during routine mouth opening before laryngoscopy. How is this unusual finding classified?
options: A common marker of difficult airway
questions.explanation: Mallampati class 0, in which the tip of the epiglottis is visible on mouth opening, occurs in about 1 to 2% of patients and is not itself a marker of easy laryngoscopy. Some patients with a visible epiglottis still have difficult views, so other predictors are still assessed.

questions.stem: Why should the patient avoid saying 'ah' during a modified Mallampati exam?
options: Phonation can falsely improve the view
questions.explanation: Saying 'ah' elevates the soft palate and can improve the view of pharyngeal structures, making the airway look more favorable than it is. The modified Mallampati examination is therefore done without phonation.

questions.stem: Which three additional measurements improve airway prediction when combined with Mallampati? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Mallampati class predicts poorly on its own, so it is combined with thyromental distance, interincisor gap, and neck circumference, along with neck mobility and history. Sternomental distance is measured with full extension, and nasal septal deviation and missing teeth affect nasal passage or mask seal rather than laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient's old record says 'Cormack-Lehane IIa with Mac 3.' A hyperangulated videolaryngoscope is planned today. How should the grade be used?
options: It is the Mallampati view before induction
It was a DL view, so the VL view may differ
It measures mouth opening and jaw protrusion
questions.explanation: Cormack-Lehane grades describe the glottic view obtained during laryngoscopy with a specific device, from grade I (full view) to grade IV (no glottis or epiglottis). A IIa view with a Mac 3 is useful history, but a hyperangulated videolaryngoscope often gives a better view. It does not describe the preoperative oral exam or mask ventilation.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy, a patient's entire glottis including the anterior commissure is seen. A bougie is offered. What is the best response?
options: Grade IIa; load the bougie first
Grade I; use the bougie routinely
Grade I; pass the tube directly
questions.explanation: A full view of the glottis including the anterior commissure is Cormack-Lehane grade I, which predicts easy intubation, so the tube can be passed under direct vision. A bougie is most useful for grade IIb or III views, and BURP helps when only the posterior structures are seen.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy of a patient, the posterior half of the cords and the arytenoids are seen. What grade is this, and what usually follows?
options: Grade IIa; intubation is usually easy
Grade IIb; a bougie is usually required
Grade I; the full glottis is in view
questions.explanation: Seeing part of the vocal cords along with the arytenoids is Cormack-Lehane grade IIa, and intubation is usually straightforward. Grade IIb shows only the arytenoids or posterior commissure without the cords and behaves more like grade III. Grade III shows only the epiglottis.

questions.stem: During RSI, direct laryngoscopy shows the epiglottis but no part of the glottis. What grade is this, and which adjunct fits best?
options: Grade III; bougie under the epiglottis
Grade IIb; pass the tube directly
questions.explanation: Cormack-Lehane grade III shows only the epiglottis, so a bougie directed anteriorly under it, external laryngeal manipulation, or a videolaryngoscope is used. Grade IV shows neither epiglottis nor glottis. Ventilation is still possible, so cricothyrotomy is not indicated, and blind tube passage risks trauma and esophageal placement.

questions.stem: Neither the epiglottis nor glottis is visible during direct laryngoscopy. Which Cormack-Lehane grade is this?
questions.explanation: Grade IV means neither the epiglottis nor the glottis is visible, which makes direct intubation unlikely to succeed without changing technique. Repositioning, a video laryngoscope, or a supraglottic or flexible scope approach is needed rather than repeated attempts.

questions.stem: After induction, direct laryngoscopy shows only the arytenoids (grade IIb). How does this view compare with grade IIa for the likely course?
options: IIb acts like grade I; proceed as normal
IIb means the airway is lost; perform a cric
IIb acts more like grade III; plan a bougie
IIb requires waking the patient at once
questions.explanation: Grades I and IIa are generally associated with easy intubation, while grade IIb, showing only the arytenoids, has a failure rate closer to grade III, so a bougie or external laryngeal manipulation is planned. Ventilation is still possible, so a front-of-neck airway or waking the patient is not indicated yet.

questions.stem: A student reviews 200 adult intubation records with direct laryngoscopy. Which Cormack-Lehane grade will appear most often?
questions.explanation: Grade II, seeing part of the vocal cords, is the most common laryngoscopic view in adults, followed by grade I. Grades III and IV are uncommon, together only a small percentage, but they account for most difficult intubations. A student who assumes most views are grade I will overestimate how often the full glottis is seen.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy reveals no useful glottic view. Which next step best changes airway geometry rather than repeating the same failed attempt?
options: Apply cricoid pressure and repeat unchanged
Pass a bougie through visible cords
Repeat blindly with the same blade
questions.explanation: A grade IV view means repeating the same approach is unlikely to work, so the next attempt should change something meaningful, such as head and neck position, blade type, external laryngeal manipulation, or a video laryngoscope. Repeated unchanged attempts increase trauma and the risk of a cannot-intubate situation.

questions.stem: A preoperative thyromental distance is recorded as 5.5 cm, measured with the patient's head neutral and mouth open. What is the best next step?
options: Record it as short and plan awake intubation
Remeasure with head extended, mouth closed
Remeasure with head neutral, mouth closed
Remeasure from the hyoid to the mentum
questions.explanation: Thyromental distance is measured from the thyroid notch to the mentum with the head fully extended and the mouth closed, so a value taken with the head neutral and mouth open is not valid. Correcting only the mouth position still leaves the head neutral, and the hyoid-to-mentum span is a different measure from the 3-3-2 rule.

questions.stem: A patient has a thyromental distance of 4 cm with full extension and Mallampati II. What does the thyromental finding suggest?
options: Caudal larynx from a long neck
Large tongue relative to the mouth
questions.explanation: A normal thyromental distance is at least about 6 cm, so 4 cm means a small mandibular space with too little room to displace the tongue and an anterior larynx that is hard to see. A caudal larynx gives a long distance instead, and atlanto-occipital extension and tongue size are measured by other tests.

questions.stem: A tall patient with a long neck has a thyromental distance of 10 cm and an unexpected grade III view on direct laryngoscopy. Which explanation fits?
questions.explanation: A thyromental distance over about 9 cm can reflect a caudally positioned larynx that is deep and hard to reach or see with a standard blade, so both extremes of thyromental distance can predict difficulty. A high anterior larynx and a small mandibular space produce a short thyromental distance.

questions.stem: A patient with retrognathia has a thyromental distance of 4 cm. Why does this anatomy increase laryngoscopy difficulty?
options: Too little space to displace the tongue
The vocal cords sit too far posterior
The larynx sits too low in the neck
questions.explanation: With retrognathia and a short thyromental distance, the mandibular space is too small to hold the displaced tongue, so the tongue stays between the blade and the larynx and blocks the glottic view. Video laryngoscopy or awake techniques may be needed.

questions.stem: Which two conditions are associated with abnormal thyromental distance? (Select 2)
options: Rheumatoid arthritis of the cervical spine
questions.explanation: Abnormal thyromental distance reflects mandibular size and laryngeal position, as with mandibular hypoplasia, and is associated with OSA. Acromegaly and hypothyroidism cause macroglossia, rheumatoid arthritis limits neck mobility, and obesity affects mask ventilation, so each makes the airway harder through a different mechanism.

questions.stem: During an airway exam, a patient has 3 fingerbreadths of mouth opening, 2 from mentum to hyoid, and 2 from hyoid to thyroid notch. What is abnormal?
options: None; each measure is within normal
questions.explanation: The 3-3-2 rule expects 3 fingerbreadths of mouth opening, 3 from mentum to hyoid, and 2 from hyoid to thyroid notch. Only 2 from mentum to hyoid means a small mandibular space, leaving less room to displace the tongue. Mouth opening and the hyoid-to-thyroid distance are normal here.

questions.stem: Before induction, a patient's hyoid-to-thyroid notch distance is 1 fingerbreadth. Which laryngoscopy finding is most likely?
options: Glottis too deep for a standard blade
Mouth too small to admit the blade
Glottis anterior to the line of sight
Tongue too large for the oral cavity
questions.explanation: Fewer than two fingerbreadths between the hyoid and thyroid notch suggests a high, anterior larynx, which sits above the line of sight during direct laryngoscopy and may need external manipulation or a videolaryngoscope. A deep larynx gives a longer distance, and mouth opening and tongue size are judged by other parts of the exam.

questions.stem: A patient with a long neck has 4 fingerbreadths from the hyoid to the thyroid notch. What adjustment may help during direct laryngoscopy?
options: BURP to bring a high larynx into view
Awake intubation for an anterior larynx
A straight blade for a floppy epiglottis
A longer blade to reach a low larynx
questions.explanation: More than two fingerbreadths between the hyoid and thyroid notch suggests a low, caudal larynx that a standard blade may not reach, so a longer blade can help. A high anterior larynx gives a short distance instead, and a floppy epiglottis is not suggested by this measurement.

questions.stem: A patient with TMJ disease can open the mouth only 2.5 cm. Which airway consequence is most likely?
options: Difficult mask ventilation from poor seal
Easy direct laryngoscopy with a Miller
questions.explanation: An interincisor opening below about 3 cm limits room to insert and manipulate a laryngoscope and pass a tube, so difficult intubation is likely and a flexible scope or nasal approach may be planned. Mask seal depends on facial features rather than mouth opening, and nasal intubation is often the preferred route.

questions.stem: A patient with acromegaly is scheduled for transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. Which airway changes should be anticipated?
questions.explanation: Acromegaly enlarges the tongue, jaw, and soft tissues of the pharynx and larynx and can narrow the glottis and subglottis, making mask ventilation and laryngoscopy hard and calling for a smaller tube. Atlantoaxial instability fits Down syndrome, micrognathia with glossoptosis fits Pierre Robin sequence, and fixed kyphosis fits ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.stem: A patient has large, protruding upper incisors. Which pair of problems do they most directly create during laryngoscopy?
options: Dental injury and blocked line of sight
Anterior larynx and a short TMD
Difficult mask seal from lip eversion
questions.explanation: Large, protruding upper incisors increase the risk of dental injury and reduce the space and line of sight between the teeth and the larynx, so a videolaryngoscope and a tooth guard may help. They do not change laryngeal position or thyromental distance, and they affect laryngoscopy more than mask seal.

questions.stem: A preoperative sternomental distance of 14 cm was measured with the patient's head neutral. What is wrong with the measurement?
options: It must be measured to the hyoid, not mentum
It must be measured from the thyroid notch
It must be measured with full head extension
It must be measured with the mouth open
questions.explanation: Sternomental distance runs from the sternal notch to the mentum with the head fully extended and the mouth closed, so it reflects both neck extension and mandibular position. A neutral-head value cannot show limited extension. Measuring from the thyroid notch gives the thyromental distance instead.

questions.stem: A patient has a sternomental distance of 11 cm in full extension and Mallampati II. How should the sternomental finding be interpreted?
options: Raises laryngoscopy risk despite Mallampati II
Reassuring, since Mallampati II overrides it
Normal, since the cutoff is about 8 cm
questions.explanation: A sternomental distance under about 12.5 cm in full extension is associated with difficult laryngoscopy, reflecting limited neck extension or a small mandible. No single test overrides another, so a reassuring Mallampati class does not cancel it. The measurement predicts laryngoscopy rather than mask ventilation.

questions.stem: During a preoperative exam, a patient's sternomental distance increases only 3 cm from neutral to full extension. How should this be interpreted?
options: Normal change; extension adds about 3 cm
Limited mouth opening; SGA may fail
Limited neck mobility; DL may be harder
Normal change if the total exceeds 20 cm
questions.explanation: A change in sternomental distance of less than about 5 cm from neutral to full extension suggests limited neck mobility, which makes aligning the airway axes harder during direct laryngoscopy. A 3 cm change is therefore abnormal, regardless of the total distance. Mouth opening is assessed separately with the interincisor gap.

questions.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint normally allows about 35 degrees of extension, which helps align the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes for direct laryngoscopy. Losing most of it, as in rheumatoid arthritis, predicts a poor direct view. A videolaryngoscope or flexible scope may be planned, but the nasal route is not mandatory.

questions.stem: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has a fixed cervical flexion deformity and cannot extend the neck. Which approach is preferred for tracheal intubation?
questions.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis can fix the neck in flexion and make direct laryngoscopy and mask ventilation difficult, so awake flexible-scope intubation keeps spontaneous breathing while the airway is secured without neck movement. Laryngoscopy after induction risks a lost airway, blind nasal attempts are unreliable, and cricothyrotomy is for rescue.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old without arthritis has less neck movement than in youth. About how much cervical flexion-extension is typically lost with aging, and what follows?
questions.explanation: Cervical flexion and extension decrease by roughly 20% from adolescence to old age, which contributes to more difficult laryngoscopy in older adults. Arthritis or prior cervical surgery reduces mobility further. The loss is meaningful but not large enough to make awake intubation routine or direct laryngoscopy impossible.

questions.stem: Which two conditions commonly reduce atlanto-occipital mobility? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Degenerative cervical disease and cervical trauma or fusion reduce atlanto-occipital mobility, as do rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. TMJ ankylosis limits mouth opening rather than neck extension, mandibular hypoplasia shortens the thyromental distance, and obesity and hypothyroidism affect soft tissue and the tongue.

questions.stem: A patient in a halo fixator has essentially no cervical motion. Which intubation approaches best minimize the need for neck movement?
questions.explanation: With a halo fixator, the neck cannot be extended, so a video laryngoscope or flexible endoscopic intubation, often awake, is preferred because they do not need alignment of the airway axes. The halo vest wrench must be available to remove the front of the frame in an emergency.

questions.stem: During airway assessment, a patient can open widely but cannot advance the lower incisors beyond the upper incisors. Which function is the upper lip bite test primarily assessing?
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test assesses how far the mandible can protrude forward, which reflects temporomandibular joint mobility and the ability to displace the tongue during laryngoscopy. It complements Mallampati class and thyromental distance.

questions.stem: A patient cannot bring the lower incisors into contact with the upper lip despite adequate mouth opening. How should this ULBT finding change your airway assessment?
options: Class B; laryngoscopy is likely easy
Class C; mask ventilation is predicted to be easy
Class A; laryngoscopy is likely easy
Class C; difficult laryngoscopy is more likely
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test reflects mandibular protrusion and temporomandibular-joint mobility. Inability to bring the lower incisors to the upper lip is class C and indicates restricted protrusion, increasing the likelihood of difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: During the upper lip bite test, the lower incisors extend above the vermilion border of the upper lip. Which class is present?
questions.explanation: In the upper lip bite test, class A means the lower incisors can bite above the vermilion border of the upper lip, showing good mandibular protrusion and predicting easier laryngoscopy. Class B reaches below the vermilion line, and class C cannot reach the upper lip.

questions.stem: An edentulous patient has a reassuring Mallampati score, but the upper lip bite test cannot be interpreted reliably. What is the main limitation?
options: Edentulous patients usually have reduced cervical motion
The maneuver depends on the lower incisors
The maneuver isolates neck extension rather than jaw movement
Edentulous status itself predicts a difficult laryngoscopy
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test depends on the lower incisors reaching the upper lip, so it cannot be interpreted reliably in edentulous patients. Other predictors, such as thyromental distance, mouth opening, and mandibular protrusion assessed without teeth, must carry more weight.

questions.stem: Two patients have identical Mallampati scores. One has a 46-cm neck circumference. What does that additional finding imply?
options: It is reassuring if mouth opening is normal
It adds concern for airway difficulty
It has no independent airway relevance
questions.explanation: A neck circumference over about 43 cm, especially in obesity and OSA, is associated with difficult laryngoscopy and mask ventilation independent of Mallampati class. It reflects excess soft tissue in the pharynx and anterior neck.

questions.stem: Which TWO findings should increase concern for difficult direct laryngoscopy despite otherwise normal vital signs? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A prominent overbite and a high, narrow palate reduce the space for the blade and the line of sight, predicting difficult laryngoscopy. A thyromental distance over 6 cm, mouth opening over 3 cm, Mallampati II, and a neck circumference under 40 cm are reassuring findings.

questions.stem: A patient has several predictors of difficult laryngoscopy. A trainee argues that planned videolaryngoscopy makes the preoperative airway exam unnecessary. Which response is BEST?
options: Videolaryngoscopy replaces assessment in elective cases
Only Mallampati becomes irrelevant; thyromental distance remains mandatory
Videolaryngoscopy makes an airway exam unnecessary if oxygenation is normal
Videolaryngoscopy changes device choice but does not replace airway assessment
questions.explanation: Video laryngoscopy improves glottic views and has reduced the predictive value of some traditional tests, but assessment still identifies risks of difficult mask ventilation, supraglottic airway placement, and front-of-neck access. It also guides backup planning and the choice of an awake technique.

questions.stem: Before surgery, a clinician measures from the mandible-neck junction to the thyroid notch and finds 1.5 fingerbreadths. What is being measured, and what does it suggest?
questions.explanation: The modified hyomental distance runs from the mandible-neck junction to the thyroid notch and estimates laryngeal position, so a short value suggests a high, anterior larynx. Thyromental distance starts at the mentum, sternomental distance starts at the sternal notch, and neither measure assesses mouth opening.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati II, a short thyromental distance, limited neck extension, and prominent upper incisors. What is the most important planning implication?
options: Mallampati II rules out difficult laryngoscopy
Several poor signs need a difficult-airway plan
Awake intubation is required with two signs
questions.explanation: No single bedside airway test reliably predicts difficulty, so several unfavorable findings raise concern even when Mallampati class is reassuring. The plan integrates all predictors, rescue options, and the consequences of failed ventilation or intubation.

questions.stem: Which FOUR findings increase the likelihood that bag-mask ventilation will be difficult? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Snoring or OSA, obesity, a beard, and edentulism make mask ventilation difficult by impairing the seal or increasing upper airway collapse, as do age over about 55 and Mallampati III or IV, summarized by MOANS. A prominent overbite predicts difficult laryngoscopy rather than difficult mask ventilation, and age 45 is below the MOANS threshold.

questions.stem: Which patient has the strongest age-related contribution to difficult mask ventilation?
questions.explanation: Age over about 55 is a MOANS predictor of difficult mask ventilation because reduced tissue elasticity and muscle tone let the airway collapse more easily. The other patients are below that threshold, so age adds little to their mask ventilation risk.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has BMI 34, no beard, full dentition, and Mallampati I. Which finding predicts more difficult mask ventilation?
questions.explanation: Obesity with a BMI over about 30 is an independent predictor of difficult mask ventilation because of extra soft tissue, reduced FRC, and chest wall mass. Mallampati I, age under 55, and intact teeth are reassuring for mask ventilation.

questions.stem: After induction, mask ventilation produces minimal chest rise, a weak ETCO2 trace, and SpO2 falls to 91%. What is the best interpretation?
options: Mask ventilation is inadequate and should be escalated
Ventilation is adequate because any ETCO2 trace is sufficient
The pattern is most consistent with pulse oximeter artifact
Ventilation is adequate because saturation remains above 85%
questions.explanation: Minimal chest rise, a weak or absent capnography trace, and falling SpO2 below about 92% indicate inadequate mask ventilation. The response is prompt escalation with repositioning, an oral airway, a two-hand technique, and then a supraglottic airway or intubation.

questions.stem: Before induction, you deliberately assess external appearance, the 3-3-2 relationship, Mallampati class, obstruction, and neck mobility. Which structured assessment are you using?
questions.explanation: LEMON assesses Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2, Mallampati, Obstruction or obesity, and Neck mobility to predict difficult laryngoscopy. MOANS predicts difficult mask ventilation, RODS difficult supraglottic airway use, and SHORT difficult cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: Which FOUR findings make supraglottic airway placement or ventilation through it less reliable? (Select 4)
options: Low pulmonary compliance or stiff lungs
A large tongue with normal mouth opening
questions.explanation: Restricted mouth opening, upper airway obstruction, distorted anatomy, and stiff lungs make supraglottic airway placement or ventilation unreliable, summarized by RODS. Mallampati III and a large tongue predict difficult laryngoscopy more than SGA failure, since the device sits above the glottis.

questions.stem: A patient with prior neck surgery, radiation, and a large anterior neck tumor may require emergency front-of-neck access. Which mnemonic specifically highlights predictors of a difficult cricothyrotomy?
questions.explanation: The SHORT mnemonic predicts difficult cricothyrotomy: Surgery or disrupted anatomy, Hematoma or infection, Obesity, Radiation, and Tumor. These factors obscure landmarks and distort tissue planes, so the membrane should be identified before induction.

questions.stem: A patient has prior neck radiation and a large neck mass, making rescue front-of-neck access potentially difficult. What is the most useful step BEFORE induction?
options: Rely on palpation during the rescue
questions.explanation: Prior radiation and a neck mass can make emergency front-of-neck access difficult, so the cricothyroid membrane is identified and marked before induction, often with ultrasound. Palpation during a crisis is unreliable in a distorted neck, and inhalational induction or a chest radiograph do not prepare front-of-neck access.

questions.stem: A cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate emergency occurs in a patient with prior neck radiation and obesity. How should those factors affect the decision to perform cricothyrotomy?
questions.explanation: In a true cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate emergency, there is no absolute contraindication to emergency front-of-neck access, because the alternative is hypoxic death. Obesity and radiation increase difficulty, so a scalpel-bougie-tube technique and early decision are favored.

questions.stem: A trauma patient requires airway management and has midline cervical tenderness. Which imaging study best evaluates a suspected cervical spine fracture?
questions.explanation: CT is the preferred imaging study for suspected cervical spine fracture in adult trauma because it is more sensitive than plain films. Until clearance, manual in-line stabilization is used during airway management, and MRI is added for ligamentous or cord injury.

questions.stem: In a patient with BMI 55, the cricothyroid membrane cannot be palpated reliably before induction. Which bedside tool is most useful for localization?
questions.explanation: Point-of-care ultrasound can locate the cricothyroid membrane when it cannot be palpated, as in morbid obesity, and it can be marked before induction. Palpation techniques fail when tissue is thick, and radiographs and nasoendoscopy do not mark the skin site.

questions.stem: Preoperative airway ultrasound shows markedly increased pretracheal soft-tissue thickness. Which problem should this finding make you anticipate?
questions.explanation: Increased pretracheal soft tissue thickness on ultrasound, at the level of the vocal cords and thyrohyoid membrane, is associated with difficult laryngoscopy, especially in obesity. It suggests harder rather than easier ventilation and does not relate to IV access.

questions.stem: A department performs 44,000 general anesthetics annually. Using a major airway complication rate of about 1 in 22,000, what is the expected annual number?
questions.explanation: The NAP4 audit found major airway complications in about 1 per 22,000 general anesthetics, so a department performing 44,000 a year would expect about 2. Many events involved poor assessment, planning, or failure to use capnography.

questions.stem: If airway-related death occurs at roughly 1 per 180,000 anesthetics, what number would be expected across 180,000 anesthetics?
questions.explanation: NAP4 estimated airway-related death or brain damage at roughly 1 per 150,000 to 180,000 anesthetics, so about 1 event would be expected in 180,000. Though rare, most were judged to involve preventable factors.

questions.stem: An obstetric service performs 600 general anesthetics. If cannot-intubate, cannot-ventilate occurs about once per 300 obstetric anesthetics, how many events would be expected?
questions.explanation: With cannot-intubate, cannot-ventilate events occurring about once in 300 obstetric general anesthetics, 600 cases would be expected to include about 2. Pregnancy brings airway edema, reduced FRC, and aspiration risk, which is one reason neuraxial anesthesia is preferred.

questions.stem: Cannot-intubate, cannot-ventilate events occur in about 1 in 300 obstetric general anesthetics versus about 1 in 2,250 outside obstetrics. Approximately how do the rates compare?
options: Obstetric CICV is about 2 times higher
Obstetric CICV is about 7.5 times higher
Obstetric CICV is about 7.5 times lower
questions.explanation: Dividing 2,250 by 300 gives 7.5, so CICV is about 7.5 times more common in obstetric general anesthesia. Airway edema, breast enlargement, reduced FRC, aspiration risk, and urgency contribute.

questions.explanation: Supraglottic airway failure occurs in about 0.19 to 1.1% of insertions, so 2,000 insertions would include roughly 4 to 22 failures. Risk factors include poor dentition, male sex, obesity, and surgical table rotation.

questions.stem: Which TWO intraoperative events or conditions are specifically associated with supraglottic airway (SGA) displacement or failure? (Select 2)
options: Extreme head or neck flexion/extension after placement
questions.explanation: Intraoperative factors like surgical table rotation and extreme head/neck movement after insertion frequently cause supraglottic airway (SGA) displacement, gas leak, or mechanical failure. Conversely, airway anatomy predictors like Mallampati class, prominent overbite, or difficult direct laryngoscopy primarily impact endotracheal intubation views rather than supraglottic device performance, since SGAs sit above the glottis.

questions.stem: An emergency department airway committee asks what most reduces the much higher rate of airway catastrophes outside the OR. Which change fits best?
options: Delaying intubation until an OR is free
Using DL rather than VL to save time
questions.explanation: Airway complications causing death or brain damage are roughly 30 to 60 times more likely in the ED and ICU than in the OR, reflecting sick patients, urgency, and less consistent capnography and preparation. Applying OR standards, including waveform capnography, checklists, and preoxygenation, addresses those gaps. Delaying a needed intubation adds risk.

questions.stem: A paramedic program reviews its trauma airway data. Prehospital cricothyrotomy rates up to about what level have been reported, and what follows?
questions.explanation: Prehospital and emergency systems have reported cricothyrotomy rates up to about 11%, far higher than in the operating room, because of trauma, blood, vomit, and unprepared patients. Regular front-of-neck training is therefore essential. Rates near 50% are not reported, and videolaryngoscopy does not remove the need for surgical airways.

questions.stem: Patients with pharyngolaryngeal disease, such as tumors, are scheduled for laryngeal biopsy. About how often has difficult intubation been reported in this population?
questions.explanation: Difficult intubation has been reported in roughly a quarter of patients with pharyngolaryngeal pathology, far above the general population. These patients often need flexible nasendoscopy review, awake techniques, and a surgeon ready for front-of-neck access.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy unexpectedly fails despite a normal bedside airway exam. Flexible evaluation reveals bulky tissue at the tongue base. Which occult problem best explains the mismatch?
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsil hyperplasia at the tongue base is not visible on routine examination and can cause unanticipated difficult or impossible laryngoscopy and mask ventilation. Video laryngoscopy may not solve it, and a supraglottic airway or flexible scope evaluation may be needed.

questions.stem: Which TWO symptoms should increase suspicion for lingual tonsil hyperplasia in a patient whose routine airway exam is otherwise reassuring? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsil hyperplasia at the tongue base may cause persistent sore throat, globus sensation, dysphagia, snoring, or OSA, so these symptoms can uncover a hidden difficult airway. Nasal congestion, cord nodules, dry cough, and heartburn point to other structures.
