questions.stem: During blind intubation with a lighted stylet in a dim room, a bright, well-defined glow appears in the anterior neck below the thyroid cartilage. What does this indicate?
options: Tracheal placement of the tube tip
Esophageal placement of the tube tip
Placement in the right piriform sinus
Placement in the vallecula above the cords
questions.explanation: With a lighted stylet such as the Trachlite, a bright, well-defined glow in the anterior neck below the thyroid cartilage shows the tip in the trachea, while esophageal placement gives a dim, diffuse glow. A glow off to one side suggests the piriform sinus, and a glow above the thyroid cartilage suggests the vallecula.

questions.stem: A hospital is deciding whether to keep lighted stylets on its difficult airway cart. Why have they largely fallen out of routine use?
options: Video and flexible scopes give direct views
They perforated the trachea in most cases
questions.explanation: Lighted stylets such as the Trachlite were largely discontinued around 2009 as videolaryngoscopes and flexible scopes became widely available and gave direct visualization. They also needed dim lighting and thin neck tissue to work. Burns, cost, and routine tracheal perforation were not the reasons for their decline.

questions.stem: An airway exchange catheter is left after extubation to preserve reintubation access. Where should its distal tip ideally rest?
questions.explanation: An airway exchange catheter left after a difficult extubation should rest in the mid to distal trachea, a few centimeters above the carina, so it stays in the trachea without irritating the carina. Its depth is documented and secured.

questions.stem: Which airway exchange catheter sizes are generally well tolerated in adults when left temporarily after extubation?
questions.explanation: Adult airway exchange catheters of about 11 or 14 French are well tolerated when left in place after extubation, allowing breathing, talking, and coughing while preserving a path for reintubation. Larger catheters cause more discomfort and coughing.

questions.stem: Why is an airway exchange catheter better tolerated than a bougie when left in place after difficult extubation?
options: It is stiffer and kinks less
It seals the glottis for ventilation
It needs no fixation at the lips
questions.explanation: An airway exchange catheter is narrow, hollow, and designed to stay temporarily in the trachea while the patient breathes and talks around it, preserving a path for reintubation. It does not seal the glottis, it must be secured, and a bougie is not meant to be left in place.

questions.stem: Jet ventilation through an airway exchange catheter is planned. Why might neuromuscular relaxation be required?
options: To lower the jet driving pressure
questions.explanation: Jet ventilation through an exchange catheter needs a clear exit path for gas, and glottic closure or laryngospasm can trap gas and cause barotrauma, so relaxation may be required. It does not prevent aspiration or change driving pressure or FiO2.

questions.stem: Before railroading an ETT over an airway exchange catheter, which size relationship must be verified?
options: ETT cuff pressure to the AEC size
ETT internal diameter to AEC external diameter
ETT curvature to the AEC curvature at the glottis
ETT length to AEC length for depth
questions.explanation: Before railroading a tube over an exchange catheter, the tube's internal diameter must comfortably fit over the catheter's external diameter, and a laryngoscope is used to lift the tongue during advancement. A tight fit can cause the tube to catch or displace the catheter.

questions.stem: Which THREE scenarios are appropriate indications for flexible-scope intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Flexible scope intubation suits anticipated difficult airways, cervical spine immobilization, restricted mouth opening, and failed intubation when ventilation is possible. It takes time and needs a clear view, so CICO, heavy bleeding, and uncooperative hypoxic patients call for other rescue techniques.

questions.stem: Which THREE situations make flexible-scope intubation a poor or unsafe primary rescue technique? (Select 3)
options: Unstable cervical spine needing neutral position
questions.explanation: Epiglottitis and airway burns risk complete obstruction during scope manipulation, and a CICV emergency needs immediate oxygenation rather than a slow scope technique. Limited mouth opening and cervical instability are classic indications for a flexible scope, and secretions controlled with an antisialagogue allow a clear view.

questions.stem: During flexible-scope intubation, the tip is aligned vertically but needs lateral steering. Which movement provides that control?
questions.explanation: On a flexible bronchoscope, the thumb lever bends the tip up and down in one plane, and rotating the wrist and scope body turns that plane to steer left or right. Keeping the scope taut and the target centered makes steering more precise.

questions.stem: A prolonged flexible-scope attempt is limited by secretions and declining oxygen reserve. What is the main advantage of oxygen insufflation through the suction port?
options: Support oxygenation and clear the lens
questions.explanation: Oxygen insufflation through the suction or working channel at about 2 to 4 L/min adds supplemental oxygen and blows secretions away from the lens, extending a prolonged scope attempt. Lidocaine is given through the channel as a separate step, and insufflation does not prevent laryngospasm or decompress the stomach.

questions.stem: An awake oral flexible-scope intubation is planned in a patient who may bite the scope. Which airway adjuncts are specifically designed to protect and guide it?
questions.explanation: Williams and Ovassapian airways are oral intubating airways designed to protect the flexible scope from biting and to guide it toward the larynx in the midline. Guedel and Berman airways are standard oropharyngeal airways not designed for scope passage.

questions.stem: The flexible scope repeatedly fogs on entry despite a clear airway. Which preparation best reduces this problem?
options: Warm saline soak or antifog agent
questions.explanation: Fogging occurs when the cold lens enters warm, humid air, so warming the tip in warm saline or applying an antifog agent prevents condensation. Cold saline worsens fogging, suction removes secretions rather than condensation, and lidocaine on the lens blurs the view.

questions.stem: Which THREE features are true advantages of videolaryngoscopy over direct laryngoscopy? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Video laryngoscopy provides a magnified view, lets the team see the glottis on a monitor, and has a shorter learning curve. It costs more, blood and secretions obscure the camera, and hyperangulated blades usually need a rigid stylet.

questions.stem: Which TWO limitations should still be anticipated when choosing videolaryngoscopy? (Select 2)
options: Need for a larger mouth opening than DL
View obscured by blood or secretions
questions.explanation: Video laryngoscopes cost more, and blood or secretions can obscure the camera, and with hyperangulated blades the tube can injure the pharynx while the operator watches the screen. Most devices record images and allow team viewing, many blades fit smaller mouth openings than direct laryngoscopy, and the glottic view is usually better.

questions.stem: A styleted ETT is advanced while attention is fixed on the VL monitor, and resistance is felt before the tube appears on screen. Which injury is specifically associated with this mechanism?
options: Vocal cord paralysis from nerve stretch
Soft palate or tonsillar pillar perforation
questions.explanation: With videolaryngoscopy, the operator may watch the screen while the styleted tube is still traveling through the mouth outside the camera view. A rigid tip can therefore injure the soft palate or tonsillar pillar before it enters the camera's field of view.

questions.stem: A trainee wants to abandon direct-laryngoscopy practice because videolaryngoscopy is available. Which advice best supports safe rescue capability?
options: Maintain skills in both DL and VL
Use DL first and VL only to rescue
questions.explanation: Proficiency in both direct and video laryngoscopy is needed, since either may be the rescue when the other fails, for example when blood obscures a video camera. Regular practice with both keeps skills current.

questions.stem: A hyperangulated GlideScope gives an excellent view but a straight ETT will not follow the visualized path. What is the main reason?
options: The tube must match the steep blade curve
The blade curves only about 15 degrees
questions.explanation: A hyperangulated GlideScope blade has a steep anterior curve of about 60 degrees, so the view is around a corner that a straight tube cannot follow. A rigid stylet shaped to match the blade guides the tube to the glottis.

questions.stem: During awake videolaryngoscopy of a patient breathing warm humidified high-flow oxygen, the GlideScope image stays clear. Which feature prevents fogging?
questions.explanation: The GlideScope uses a heated lens that keeps warm, humid exhaled gas from condensing on the camera. The McGrath relies on a hydrophilic antifog coating instead, and suction or oxygen ports clear secretions or add oxygen but do not prevent condensation.

questions.stem: A McGrath videolaryngoscope is used for an intubation during patient transport with no power outlet, and the camera stays clear in humid air. Which feature prevents fogging?
options: Heated lens that warms the camera
questions.explanation: The McGrath uses a hydrophilic antifog coating on its disposable blade rather than an active heater, which suits its battery-powered, portable design with a screen on the handle. The heated lens is the GlideScope's approach, and oxygen or suction channels do not prevent condensation.

questions.stem: A teaching hospital wants one video system that offers Macintosh and Miller blades for direct and video viewing, hyperangulated blades, and recording. Which device fits?
questions.explanation: The C-MAC offers Macintosh and Miller geometry blades that allow both direct and video viewing, plus hyperangulated blades and image recording, which suits teaching and switching techniques. The GlideScope is mainly hyperangulated, the McGrath is a portable handle-screen device, and the Trachlite is a lighted stylet.

questions.stem: A videolaryngoscope is needed for intubations during patient transport and in remote areas without an external monitor. Which device fits best?
questions.explanation: The McGrath has a self-contained, rotatable screen on the handle with disposable blades, so it is compact and portable for transport and remote sites. The GlideScope and C-MAC usually use a separate monitor, and a flexible scope is a different technique that is slower in emergencies.

questions.stem: A hyperangulated GlideScope view is excellent, but tube delivery is expected to be difficult. How should the ETT be prepared?
options: No stylet and a straight, unshaped tube
questions.explanation: With a hyperangulated blade, the tube must follow a steep anterior curve, so a rigid stylet such as the GlideRite or a tube preshaped to match the blade is used. An unshaped tube cannot reach the glottis even with an excellent view.

questions.stem: During GlideScope insertion, the operator keeps looking directly into the mouth and overshoots the epiglottis. What technique would reduce this error?
options: Insert to the right and sweep the tongue
Insert laterally and look in the mouth first
Insert midline and look at the monitor early
questions.explanation: A hyperangulated blade is inserted in the midline over the tongue without a sweep, and the operator watches the monitor early to identify structures as the blade advances. Looking into the mouth too long tends to overshoot the epiglottis.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation and intubation have both failed and oxygenation cannot be restored. Which situation now mandates front-of-neck rescue?
options: Nasal intubation failure with good mask ventilation
Routine difficult intubation with good ventilation
questions.explanation: Front-of-neck access is mandated in a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate situation, when intubation, mask ventilation, and supraglottic airway attempts have all failed to restore oxygenation. Delay leads to hypoxic brain injury and cardiac arrest.

questions.stem: Which THREE scenarios are accepted indications for emergency cricothyrotomy? (Select 3)
options: Facial or neck trauma preventing oral/nasal access
Failed intubation with good mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Emergency cricothyrotomy is indicated for CICO, facial or neck trauma preventing oral or nasal access, and immediate upper airway obstruction. Laryngospasm that responds to CPAP and failed intubation with good mask ventilation still allow oxygenation, and an anticipated difficult airway calls for awake techniques.

questions.stem: Which THREE approaches represent the major cricothyrotomy techniques? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The three cricothyrotomy approaches are needle cricothyrotomy with transtracheal jet ventilation, percutaneous wire-guided (Seldinger) kits, and the open scalpel-bougie-tube technique favored in CICO. Retrograde and blind nasal intubation are translaryngeal techniques, and tracheostomy enters below the cricoid as a planned procedure.

questions.stem: During a CICO event, needle cricothyrotomy is chosen, and the only catheters at hand are 20G and 22G IV catheters. What is the main problem?
options: They are too short to reach the trachea
They are too large for the membrane
They need a 15-mm adapter to work
They kink and give too little flow
questions.explanation: Needle cricothyrotomy needs a large-bore, kink-resistant cannula, usually 14 gauge or larger and ideally purpose-made, connected to a high-pressure oxygen source. Small, soft IV catheters kink at the skin and deliver too little flow. They easily reach the trachea and fit the membrane, and connection needs a jet injector or adapter for any cannula.

questions.stem: During transtracheal jet ventilation, the chest fails to rise and the neck swells with crepitus. What has most likely happened?
options: The catheter is out of the trachea
The upper airway is fully obstructed
The jet pressure is too low
questions.explanation: Neck swelling with crepitus and no chest rise means gas is entering the subcutaneous tissue, so the catheter has left the trachea and jetting must stop. Complete upper airway obstruction would inflate the chest without exhalation, low pressure or kinking reduces flow without causing emphysema.

questions.stem: During a CICO event in an adult, a transtracheal catheter is connected to a jet injector from the wall oxygen supply. What driving pressure is typically used?
questions.explanation: Adult transtracheal jet ventilation commonly uses about 50 psi from a regulated high-pressure source, with lower pressures in children, because a small cannula needs high pressure to deliver enough flow. The airway above must allow exhalation, or barotrauma follows. Pressures of 5 to 20 psi deliver too little flow, and 200 psi is excessive.

questions.stem: During transtracheal jet ventilation, what breath frequency best limits air trapping while maintaining oxygenation?
questions.explanation: Transtracheal jet ventilation uses a low rate of about 8 to 12 breaths per minute so the lungs can empty passively through the upper airway between breaths. Faster rates cause gas trapping and barotrauma.

questions.stem: Which inspiratory-to-expiratory ratio best allows adequate passive exhalation during TTJV?
questions.explanation: An inspiratory to expiratory ratio of about 1:3 to 1:4 gives enough time for passive exhalation through the upper airway during jet ventilation. A 1:1 ratio would cause air trapping and rising intrathoracic pressure.

questions.stem: How long should each inspiratory jet generally last during TTJV?
questions.explanation: Each jet breath during TTJV lasts about 0.5 to 1 second, followed by a longer passive exhalation, with chest rise and fall watched to avoid stacking. Longer jets risk overdistension and barotrauma.

questions.stem: Before delivering the next jet breath, chest recoil has not completed. Why should the next breath be delayed?
options: To increase oxygen delivery on the next breath
To prevent air trapping and barotrauma
questions.explanation: Exhalation during TTJV is passive through the upper airway, so the next breath waits until the chest has fallen back, or gas stacks and causes air trapping, barotrauma, and hypotension. The delay is not for repositioning or confirming placement.

questions.stem: During TTJV, exhalation becomes severely impaired by upper-airway obstruction. Which complication is the most immediate life threat?
questions.explanation: With complete upper airway obstruction, gas delivered by TTJV cannot escape, so the most immediate threat is barotrauma with pneumothorax and circulatory collapse from rising intrathoracic pressure. Hypercarbia develops more slowly, and kinking or low FiO2 is not the danger described.

questions.stem: Which FOUR complications are recognized risks of TTJV, especially when gas egress is limited? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Transtracheal jet ventilation can cause barotrauma, pneumothorax, and subcutaneous emphysema when gas cannot escape, and it removes CO2 poorly, so hypercarbia develops. Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy and tracheal stenosis are linked to tracheotomy and prolonged intubation rather than to a brief transtracheal catheter.

questions.stem: Because the transtracheal catheter is used mainly for insufflation, how does exhalation normally occur during TTJV?
questions.explanation: During transtracheal jet ventilation, gas enters through the catheter and exhalation occurs passively through the patient's upper airway. If the upper airway is obstructed, gas cannot leave, which makes barotrauma likely.

questions.stem: Which THREE pieces of equipment are central to retrograde intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Retrograde intubation passes a needle or catheter through the cricothyroid membrane, threads a J-wire or suture up into the mouth, and uses Magill forceps to retrieve it so the tube can follow it down. A videolaryngoscope, rigid bronchoscope, and laser tube are used in other airway techniques.

questions.stem: During retrograde intubation, in which direction should the cricothyroid needle be angled?
questions.explanation: For retrograde intubation, the needle passes through the cricothyroid membrane angled cephalad so the guidewire travels up through the vocal cords and out of the mouth or nose. The tube is then threaded over the wire into the trachea.

questions.stem: In which situation could retrograde intubation be considered?
options: Visual intubation fails but ventilation is adequate
CICO with no ventilation possible at all
Routine elective intubation in a healthy patient
questions.explanation: Retrograde intubation can be considered when visual techniques have failed but oxygenation is maintained, since it takes several minutes. It is not appropriate in CICO, where immediate front-of-neck access is needed.

questions.stem: A patient on prolonged mechanical ventilation is scheduled for an elective surgical tracheostomy. At which level is the tracheal opening usually made, and why?
options: Cricothyroid membrane, for speed and immediate access
At the cricoid cartilage, to provide a firm anatomical landmark
Rings 7 to 9, to avoid the thyroid gland and major vessels
Rings 2 to 4, to avoid subglottic stenosis associated with cricoid cartilage damage
questions.explanation: An elective surgical tracheostomy is typically performed through an incision between the second and fourth tracheal rings. Staying below the first ring and cricoid cartilage prevents subglottic stenosis and perichondritis, which are major long-term risks if the cricoid cartilage is injured. The cricothyroid membrane is reserved for emergency surgical cricothyroidotomy, while rings 7 through 9 are too deep and positioned near the sternal notch.

questions.stem: A CICO emergency requires immediate airway access. Why is surgical tracheotomy generally not the first emergency choice?
options: It has a higher stenosis rate
It is slow and needs specialized help
It cannot accept a cuffed tube
questions.explanation: Surgical tracheotomy takes considerable time and needs a surgical team, lighting, and a controlled field, while the cricothyroid membrane is superficial and fast to reach in a CICO crisis. Stenosis risk, anesthesia, and tube type are not the reasons it is avoided as the first emergency step.

questions.stem: Which TWO complications are specifically associated with tracheotomy? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy can injure the recurrent laryngeal nerve near the trachea and, rarely, erode into the innominate artery, causing massive hemorrhage often preceded by sentinel bleeding. Facial, phrenic, thoracic duct, and vertebral artery injuries are associated with other neck procedures.

questions.stem: During a CICO event in an adult, the team prepares a scalpel-bougie-tube airway. Which structure is the target?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane is the target for emergency front-of-neck access because it is superficial, relatively avascular, and found between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. The thyrohyoid membrane is above the larynx, the cricotracheal ligament is below the cricoid, and lower tracheal rings are deeper and slower to reach.

questions.stem: In an obese patient with poorly palpable neck landmarks, how can ultrasound most directly improve FONA preparation?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound identifies the cricothyroid membrane when it cannot be palpated, as in obesity or neck masses, so it can be marked before induction. It can also confirm tube position or estimate airway size, but those do not prepare front-of-neck access, and it does not guide jet pressures.

questions.stem: Which THREE outcomes are central goals of extubation planning rather than simply removing the tube early? (Select 3)
options: Avoid using an airway exchange catheter
questions.explanation: Extubation planning aims to minimize cardiopulmonary stress, reduce respiratory complications such as reintubation and pneumonia, and shorten hospital stay and costs. Timing is chosen for safety rather than turnover or discharge speed, and an exchange catheter is a useful tool in a high-risk extubation.

questions.stem: A long neck dissection had an easy intubation, but significant edema is expected. Which principle should guide extubation?
options: Extubation carries real risk and needs a plan
questions.explanation: Extubation carries real risk, and airway edema from long head and neck surgery can make reintubation harder than the original intubation, so a plan with cuff-leak assessment, exchange catheter, delayed extubation, or tracheostomy is needed. Steroids reduce but do not remove edema, and deep extubation removes airway control.

questions.stem: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring shows a TOF ratio of 0.82 before extubation. How should this be interpreted?
options: No; the TOF ratio should exceed 0.9
Yes; a ratio above 0.3 is adequate here
Yes; a ratio above 0.5 is adequate
Yes; a ratio above 0.7 is adequate
questions.explanation: A train-of-four ratio of 0.82 indicates residual neuromuscular weakness. Extubation readiness requires quantitative recovery above 0.9 because clinically important pharyngeal and respiratory muscle weakness can persist below that threshold.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings can still be present with clinically significant residual neuromuscular blockade? (Select 3)
options: TOF ratio of 0.95 by quantitative monitoring
questions.explanation: A 5-second head lift and a normal tidal volume can return while the TOF ratio is still around 0.5, and fade cannot be felt or seen once the ratio is above about 0.4, so all three can coexist with dangerous residual block. A quantitative TOF ratio of 0.9 or more is the standard for adequate recovery, and sustained 100-Hz tetanus is one of the more sensitive clinical tests, so those indicate recovery rather than hide residual block.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient has a vital capacity of 900 mL before extubation. How does this compare with the target threshold?
options: No; it should exceed 15 mL/kg, or 1,050 mL
No; it should exceed 30 mL/kg, or 2,100 mL
questions.explanation: A vital capacity of at least about 15 mL/kg is a common extubation threshold, which is 1,050 mL for 70 kg, so 900 mL, about 13 mL/kg, is below target. Low vital capacity suggests residual weakness or poor effort and a limited ability to cough.

questions.stem: An 80-kg patient has spontaneous tidal volumes of 250 mL. Does this satisfy the usual extubation target?
options: No; the target is 10 to 12 mL/kg
No; the target is 4 to 5 mL/kg
questions.explanation: Spontaneous tidal volume should be at least about 4 to 5 mL/kg, or 320 to 400 mL for 80 kg, before extubation, so 250 mL, about 3 mL/kg, is inadequate. Low volumes suggest residual weakness or opioid effect.

questions.stem: On FiO2 0.40, a patient's SpO2 is 93% and PaO2 is 72 mmHg. Do these values meet common extubation oxygenation criteria?
questions.explanation: Common oxygenation criteria for extubation are an SpO2 above about 90% and a PaO2 above about 60 mmHg on an FiO2 below 0.5, so these values are acceptable. Higher oxygen requirements suggest the patient may not tolerate extubation.

questions.stem: Which FOUR global conditions should be present before extubation? (Select 4)
options: Return of laryngeal and cough reflexes
questions.explanation: Before extubation, the patient should be hemodynamically stable, normothermic, with adequate neuromuscular strength and returned airway reflexes such as cough and swallow. Full cognitive recovery and a tidal volume above 10 mL/kg are stricter than needed; about 5 mL/kg and following commands are typical targets.

questions.stem: A patient meets standard extubation criteria but develops respiratory failure minutes after extubation. What does this illustrate about extubation?
options: Extubation is a functional test of stability
Criteria predict success with absolute certainty
questions.explanation: Extubation is itself a functional test of whether spontaneous ventilation, airway patency, and cardiopulmonary reserve can be sustained, so failure can occur despite met criteria and monitoring continue. Criteria lower risk but do not predict success with certainty.

questions.stem: At the end of a tonsillectomy, a child begins coughing and breath-holding, with dilated pupils and roving eyes. Why should extubation be delayed?
options: Stage I; analgesia is still present
questions.explanation: Breath-holding, coughing, dilated pupils, and roving eyes mark Guedel stage II, when airway reflexes are hyperactive and laryngospasm and vomiting are likely, so extubation waits until the child is fully awake or is done deep in stage III. Stage III would not show these signs, and stage IV is overdose.

questions.stem: For a routine patient, which timing choices are generally safest for extubation?
options: During stage II excitement, as reflexes return
As soon as spontaneous breathing starts
Deeply anesthetized (stage III) or fully awake
questions.explanation: Extubation is safest either deep in stage III, when airway reflexes are suppressed, or fully awake with reflexes recovered, avoiding the excitable stage II. Deep extubation is reserved for patients with easy airways and low aspiration risk.

questions.stem: A patient is at high risk for reintubation difficulty. When should extubation occur?
options: When reflexes return and ventilation is adequate
Deep in stage III to avoid any coughing on the tube
questions.explanation: Patients at risk of difficult reintubation should be extubated fully awake, with airway reflexes and adequate ventilation restored, so they can protect and maintain their own airway. Deep extubation removes that safety margin.

questions.stem: Which FOUR drug classes can blunt the cardiovascular response to awake extubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers such as esmolol, calcium channel blockers, vasodilators such as nitroglycerin, and alpha-blockers blunt the hypertension and tachycardia of awake extubation. Benzodiazepines sedate without reliably blunting the sympathetic surge, and anticholinergics raise heart rate.

questions.stem: Which THREE strategies can reduce coughing and straining during extubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: IV lidocaine, intracuff lidocaine, and cautious low-dose opioids reduce coughing and straining on the tube during emergence. Ketamine can increase secretions and airway reactivity, and neostigmine and atropine do not suppress cough.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of airway complications in large audits occur at extubation or during recovery?
questions.explanation: Audits such as NAP4 found that up to about a third of major airway complications occurred at emergence or in recovery, from obstruction, laryngospasm, residual weakness, edema, or lost access. Extubation therefore needs the same planning as induction.

questions.stem: Which FOUR techniques are reasonable for extubating a high-risk airway while preserving rescue options? (Select 4)
options: Use of an airway exchange catheter
questions.explanation: High-risk extubation keeps a route back: delayed extubation, extubation over a flexible scope, exchange to an SGA (Bailey maneuver), or leaving an airway exchange catheter in place. Deep extubation removes airway control in a patient who may be hard to reintubate, and stage II extubation risks laryngospasm.

questions.stem: Before extubating a known difficult airway, what team action is most important?
options: Keep backup gear outside the room
questions.explanation: Before extubating a known difficult airway, the team discusses the plan, signs of failure, and rescue roles, with equipment at the bedside. Speed does not replace preparation, and deciding on rescue after extubation wastes the time needed if it fails.

questions.stem: Which FOUR patient factors increase the risk of difficult extubation or reintubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Generalized airway edema, limited cervical mobility, tracheomalacia, and OSA increase the risk of difficult extubation or reintubation, as does a known difficult intubation. Controlled hypertension and mild intermittent asthma do not add this risk.

questions.stem: Which THREE patients are at greatest risk for a difficult extubation? (Select 3)
options: After a short laparoscopy in a patient with GERD
After laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a grade I view
After anterior cervical fusion at three levels
After a 2-hour breast case with controlled asthma
After total thyroidectomy with possible nerve injury
After 6 hours prone with marked facial edema
questions.explanation: Difficult extubation risk comes from conditions that compromise the airway after the tube is out: recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hematoma after thyroidectomy, airway edema after long prone cases, and prevertebral swelling or hematoma after multilevel anterior cervical surgery. GERD raises aspiration concern and asthma raises bronchospasm concern at extubation, but neither predicts loss of a patent airway the way edema or cord dysfunction does.

questions.stem: Which FOUR anesthetic factors should increase concern about extubation failure? (Select 4)
options: Use of a cuffed tube at 22 cmH2O
questions.explanation: Difficult or traumatic intubation, laryngotracheal trauma, excessive fluid resuscitation, and absence of a cuff leak all point to airway edema and higher risk of extubation failure. A brief case and a cuff kept at 20 to 30 cmH2O are routine and do not add risk; edema findings may prompt steroids or extubation over an exchange catheter.

questions.stem: A patient has no cuff leak after prolonged airway surgery. What is the most concerning interpretation?
options: It suggests an overfilled cuff only
questions.explanation: Absence of a cuff leak after deflating the cuff following prolonged airway surgery suggests swollen laryngeal or tracheal tissue may obstruct the airway after extubation, prompting delay, steroids, or an exchange catheter. It does not reflect reversal, and the test is done with the cuff deflated.

questions.stem: Which THREE complications are consistent with residual neuromuscular blockade after extubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Residual neuromuscular blockade weakens the pharyngeal muscles, causing upper airway obstruction, hypoxemia, and aspiration, and it blunts the carotid body response to hypoxia. Hypertension, bronchospasm, and opioid-related delayed emergence can occur after anesthesia but are not produced by residual blockade itself.

questions.stem: After a short case with rocuronium, TOF count is 1, and sugammadex 4 mg/kg is given with full recovery in about 2 minutes. What mechanism explains the speed?
questions.explanation: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium in plasma, creating a gradient that pulls drug away from the junction, so recovery is fast even from deep blockade. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and has a ceiling effect, and sugammadex neither stimulates receptors nor increases acetylcholine release.

questions.stem: Immediately after extubation, the patient makes forceful inspiratory efforts but no air moves and the cords are tightly closed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is an involuntary, sustained closure of the vocal cords, and complete laryngospasm shows forceful inspiratory effort with no air movement and no sound. It differs from bronchospasm, which causes wheezing and prolonged expiration.

questions.stem: During emergence, a 4-year-old develops complete laryngospasm. Why is rapid treatment especially urgent in this child?
options: Small oxygen reserve; desaturation is common
questions.explanation: Oxygen desaturation develops in a large share of laryngospasm episodes, reported in up to about 60%, and children have high oxygen consumption and small FRC, so SpO2 falls fast. Hypoxemia then causes bradycardia, and negative-pressure pulmonary edema can follow. Treatment proceeds from CPAP and jaw thrust to propofol or succinylcholine without delay.

questions.stem: During light anesthesia, secretions touch the vocal cords and the glottis clamps shut. Which reflex arc is responsible?
options: SLN afferent to RLN motor response
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is a reflex in which stimulation of the supraglottic and glottic mucosa travels through the internal superior laryngeal nerve and triggers adduction through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal-to-vagal pathway mediates the gag reflex, and the other pathways do not control the glottis.

questions.stem: After extubation, a patient makes vigorous inspiratory effort with no air movement and no stridor, and jaw thrust with CPAP fails at first. Which mechanism best describes this?
questions.explanation: Complete laryngospasm involves extrinsic laryngeal muscles pulling the supraglottic tissues closed over the glottis like a ball valve, so there is no air movement and no sound. The glottic shutter is partial closure by intrinsic muscles that still allows stridor, bronchospasm produces wheeze, and cord paralysis causes stridor with some flow.

questions.stem: After extubation, a patient has high-pitched inspiratory stridor with some air movement. Which mechanism best describes this?
questions.explanation: Partial laryngospasm is the glottic shutter, in which intrinsic laryngeal muscles partly close the cords so some air moves with inspiratory stridor, and CPAP with jaw thrust often relieves it. Ball-valve closure is complete with no air movement, tracheomalacia usually causes expiratory noise, and bronchospasm causes expiratory wheeze.

questions.stem: Which THREE conditions commonly trigger laryngospasm around extubation? (Select 3)
options: Blood or secretions on the cords
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is triggered by airway manipulation, blood or secretions on the cords, and light anesthesia during stage II. Extubating deep after suctioning or fully awake avoids the excitable stage, and IV lidocaine lowers airway reactivity, so these reduce rather than trigger laryngospasm.

questions.stem: Persistent laryngospasm continues despite CPAP. Jaw thrust plus firm pressure at the laryngospasm notch is applied. Which maneuver is being used?
questions.explanation: The Larson maneuver applies firm inward and anterior pressure at the laryngospasm notch, between the mandibular ramus and mastoid process, combined with jaw thrust and CPAP, to help break laryngospasm. Propofol or succinylcholine follow if it persists.

questions.stem: Laryngospasm persists despite airway-opening maneuvers and positive pressure, and SpO2 continues to fall. Which medication should be given next?
questions.explanation: If laryngospasm persists despite CPAP and jaw thrust and saturation keeps falling, a small IV dose of succinylcholine, about 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg, relaxes the cords, with atropine ready in children. Naloxone, lidocaine, and glycopyrrolate do not break established spasm.

questions.stem: After a severe laryngospasm episode with strong inspiratory efforts against a closed glottis, which pulmonary complication is a major concern?
questions.explanation: Strong inspiratory efforts against a closed glottis create very negative intrathoracic pressure, which raises transmural capillary pressure and causes negative-pressure pulmonary edema, often with pink frothy secretions. Stenosis develops later, and pneumothorax and embolism are not the expected result.

questions.stem: A child develops inspiratory stridor after extubation due to subglottic edema. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Postextubation croup is inflammation and edema of the subglottic region after intubation, causing inspiratory stridor and a barking cough, most often in children, whose narrow subglottis magnifies the effect of swelling. Vocal cord paralysis and bronchospasm present differently.

questions.stem: Which TWO findings most strongly support postextubation croup rather than bronchospasm? (Select 2)
options: Rising peak airway pressure on the ventilator
questions.explanation: Inspiratory stridor and a barking cough point to subglottic edema from postextubation croup. Expiratory wheeze, a prolonged expiratory phase, and improvement after albuterol all point to lower airway bronchospasm, and rising peak pressure applies to a ventilated patient. Croup is treated with racemic epinephrine and steroids.

questions.stem: A child is extubated uneventfully but develops barky cough and stridor shortly afterward. When does postextubation croup most commonly appear?
questions.explanation: Postextubation croup usually appears within about 3 hours of extubation, often within the first hour, so children are observed in PACU long enough to detect it. Late-onset stridor suggests another cause.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors increase the risk of postextubation croup? (Select 4)
options: Airway edema from trauma or positioning
Use of a cuffed tube in an adult
Use of a tube with an audible leak at 20 cmH2O
questions.explanation: Multiple intubation attempts, an oversized tube, excessive head and neck movement, and airway trauma or edema all raise the risk of postextubation croup. A leak at 20 cmH2O suggests the tube is not oversized, and cuffed tubes in adults at proper pressure are standard.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops a barky cough and stridor in PACU. Which nebulized racemic epinephrine dose is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Nebulized racemic epinephrine 2.25%, typically 0.05 mL/kg up to 0.5 mL diluted in about 2.5 to 3 mL of saline, reduces subglottic edema through mucosal vasoconstriction. Effects last about 2 hours with possible rebound, so the child is observed for several hours.

questions.explanation: Dexamethasone at about 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg reduces airway edema in croup, so a 15-kg child would receive about 1.5 to 7.5 mg. Its effect takes a few hours, so racemic epinephrine is used for immediate relief.

questions.stem: A child with postextubation croup remains stridorous after racemic epinephrine, and heliox 70:30 is started. Why does it help?
options: It delivers more oxygen than 100% O2
questions.explanation: Helium is much less dense than nitrogen, and resistance to turbulent flow through a narrowed airway depends on gas density, so heliox lowers the work of breathing across the edematous segment. It has no anti-inflammatory effect, its viscosity is similar to air, and its oxygen fraction is lower than 100% oxygen.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old and an adult each develop 1 mm of subglottic edema after intubation. Why is the child's obstruction much worse?
options: The child's subglottis is wider than the glottis
The child has lower oxygen consumption
The child's trachea is more rigid
Resistance rises steeply as small radius falls
questions.explanation: Resistance to laminar flow varies with the fourth power of the radius, so 1 mm of edema narrows a small pediatric subglottis far more in proportion than an adult airway, and in infants it can cut the cross-sectional area by more than half. The child's subglottis is the narrowest point, oxygen consumption is higher, and the trachea is more compliant.

questions.stem: During consent, a patient with loose upper incisors asks about airway injuries. Which injury leads anesthesia airway malpractice claims?
questions.explanation: Dental injury is the most common airway-related anesthesia malpractice claim, usually involving the upper incisors during laryngoscopy, emergence biting, or oral airway use. Preexisting dental disease such as loose teeth should be documented and discussed during consent. Esophageal perforation, cord paralysis, and arytenoid dislocation are more serious but much less common.

questions.stem: During laryngoscopy, which teeth are most vulnerable to injury from improper blade leverage?
options: Mandibular molars on the right side
questions.explanation: The maxillary central incisors are most often injured because they are used as a fulcrum when the laryngoscope is levered backward. Lifting along the handle and using tooth guards or video laryngoscopes in patients with fragile teeth reduces the risk.

questions.stem: Weeks after a difficult intubation, a patient remains hoarse with a weak voice. Which THREE laryngeal injuries could explain this? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Persistent hoarseness after a difficult intubation can come from vocal cord paralysis due to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, granuloma or polyp formation at the vocal processes, or arytenoid dislocation. Pharyngeal abrasions heal in days, lingual nerve injury causes tongue numbness, and carinal tracheomalacia does not alter the voice.

questions.stem: After traumatic intubation, which combination of findings should raise concern for esophageal perforation?
questions.explanation: Esophageal or pharyngeal perforation after traumatic intubation presents with neck swelling, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, and later fever and sore throat. Hoarseness alone suggests cord injury, wheezing suggests bronchospasm, and stridor responsive to racemic epinephrine suggests edema.

questions.stem: Why does suspected esophageal perforation require urgent treatment even after the airway has been secured?
options: The main consequence is transient dysphagia
Aspiration pneumonia is the main risk
questions.explanation: Untreated esophageal perforation can lead to mediastinitis, which carries a mortality as high as about 50%, so early recognition, antibiotics, and surgical evaluation are urgent. Dysphagia and stenosis are not the main threat, and aspiration is not the mechanism of harm.

questions.stem: Which THREE practices increase the risk of tracheal injury during or after intubation? (Select 3)
options: Video laryngoscopy on the first attempt
A 7.0 ETT in an average adult woman
A stylet protruding past the tube tip
questions.explanation: Tracheal injury comes from mechanical trauma and mucosal ischemia: a stylet tip that extends past the tube can tear the trachea, repeated attempts multiply trauma, and cuff pressures above about 30 cmH2O exceed mucosal capillary perfusion. A cuff pressure of 25 cmH2O is within the recommended 20 to 30 range, a 7.0 tube is appropriately sized for an average woman, and a successful first-pass video laryngoscopy reduces trauma.

questions.stem: Clinically significant pulmonary aspiration during anesthesia is uncommon. Approximately how often does it occur?
questions.explanation: Clinically significant aspiration occurs in roughly 1 in 35,000 anesthetics overall, with higher rates in emergency surgery, obstetrics, and patients with delayed gastric emptying. Most aspiration occurs at induction or emergence.

questions.stem: After gastric aspiration, what is the expected sequence of lung injury?
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonitis begins with direct chemical injury from acidic gastric contents. A secondary inflammatory response then develops, which can worsen pulmonary edema, gas-exchange impairment, and respiratory dysfunction after the initial insult.

questions.stem: During mask ventilation of a full-stomach patient, which pressure range should generally not be exceeded to limit gastric insufflation and aspiration risk?
questions.explanation: Keeping mask ventilation pressures below about 15 to 20 cmH2O limits gas entry into the stomach, since the lower esophageal sphincter opens at roughly 20 cmH2O, which reduces regurgitation and aspiration risk. Gentle, small breaths are used when mask ventilation is needed in a full-stomach patient.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis is scheduled for GA. Which FOUR medications can reduce aspiration risk or severity? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Famotidine and omeprazole reduce acid production, sodium citrate neutralizes acid already present, and metoclopramide speeds gastric emptying, lowering the volume and acidity of gastric contents. Glycopyrrolate does not reliably raise pH, and ondansetron treats nausea without changing gastric volume or acidity.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease and suspected gastric stasis needs aspiration prophylaxis. Which commonly used prokinetic should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide blocks central dopamine receptors in addition to its prokinetic effect, so it can worsen parkinsonian rigidity and tremor and is avoided in Parkinson disease. Acid-reducing agents such as famotidine, omeprazole, and sodium citrate are safe.

questions.stem: After intubation, chest rise and bilateral breath sounds are present but are not definitive. Which finding most reliably confirms tracheal placement?
questions.explanation: Chest movement and breath sounds can occur with esophageal intubation, while a sustained exhaled CO2 waveform over several breaths is the most reliable routine confirmation of tracheal placement. During cardiac arrest, low flow can reduce the CO2 signal.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings may falsely reassure the provider about ETT placement and therefore should not be used alone? (Select 3)
options: Tube seen passing between the cords
questions.explanation: Bilateral breath sounds, chest wall movement, and tube condensation can all occur with esophageal intubation, so they should not be used alone to confirm placement. Sustained capnography over several breaths and direct visualization of the tube between the cords or of tracheal rings are reliable.

questions.stem: After intubation of a patient in cardiac arrest, ETCO2 is low and equivocal. Which method best confirms tracheal placement?
options: Chest radiograph showing the tube's tip depth
Bilateral breath sounds with chest rise
questions.explanation: During low-flow states, ETCO2 can be low even with tracheal placement, so seeing tracheal rings and the carina through a flexible bronchoscope confirms placement and depth. A chest radiograph shows depth but cannot exclude esophageal placement, and breath sounds and chest rise can occur with esophageal intubation.

questions.stem: Which THREE complications are expected from traumatic or unrecognized esophageal intubation? (Select 3)
options: Gastric distention with a rising ETCO2
questions.explanation: Trauma to the esophagus can perforate it, letting air track into the neck and chest as subcutaneous emphysema, and contamination of the mediastinum leads to mediastinitis. Gastric distention does occur, but exhaled CO2 is absent or fades, not rising, which is why capnography detects the error. Bronchospasm and one-lung atelectasis are complications of a tracheal tube, not an esophageal one.

questions.stem: A patient's SpO2 falls 5 minutes after an intubation that produced breath sounds and chest rise, but no ETCO2 waveform was ever seen. Which error must be excluded first?
questions.explanation: Breath sounds and chest movement can mislead, and an absent capnogram after intubation means esophageal placement until proven otherwise, which is why unrecognized esophageal intubation is a major cause of severe respiratory claims. A right mainstem tube, bronchospasm, or pneumothorax would still produce exhaled CO2.

questions.stem: Which THREE complications should remain on the immediate differential after tracheal intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: After intubation, airway trauma, aspiration, and endobronchial or esophageal tube placement are the immediate airway causes of desaturation, high pressures, or bleeding. Malignant hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, and pulmonary embolism are possible intraoperative events but are not complications of the intubation itself.

questions.stem: Which THREE practices reduce airway-management complications during repeated or difficult intubation? (Select 3)
options: Using a larger tube to reduce resistance
Rapid repeated attempts to shorten apnea
Filling the cuff until the leak stops
questions.explanation: Careful technique with properly sized devices, limiting laryngoscopy attempts, and measuring cuff pressure reduce trauma, edema, and later complications. A larger tube increases mucosal injury, repeated rapid attempts worsen edema and bleeding, and filling until the leak stops often overinflates the cuff.

questions.stem: A bearded patient with BMI 38, OSA, Mallampati IV, TMD 5 cm, and neck circumference 46 cm presents for GA. Which THREE airway tasks are predicted to be difficult? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Beard, obesity, and OSA predict difficult bag-mask ventilation; Mallampati IV and a 5 cm thyromental distance predict difficult laryngoscopy; and a 46 cm neck obscures cricothyroid landmarks. SGA placement and nasal scope intubation are less affected by these findings, and extubation readiness depends on events during the case.

questions.stem: A patient with a beard, BMI 42, Mallampati IV, limited neck extension, and a thick neck presents for surgery. Which preinduction strategy best preserves options if intubation fails?
options: Standard induction with a Mac 3 blade
Awake intubation or VL, SGA, and FONA ready
Induce and place an LMA first
questions.explanation: Several predictors point to difficult mask ventilation, laryngoscopy, and front-of-neck access, so awake intubation is considered, or induction proceeds only with a videolaryngoscope, SGA, and marked front-of-neck access ready. Standard induction, inhalation induction, or a planned LMA leaves no prepared rescue if ventilation fails.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient will receive topical lidocaine. Using 4.5 mg/kg as the working maximum, what is the approximate total dose limit?
questions.explanation: Using 4.5 mg/kg as the working maximum, a 70-kg patient may receive about 315 mg of lidocaine, and since 4% lidocaine contains 40 mg/mL, that is about 7.9 mL of 4%. Doses from all routes are added together.

questions.stem: You draw up 5 mL of 4% lidocaine for topicalization. How many milligrams does this contain?
questions.explanation: A 4% solution contains 40 mg/mL, so 5 mL contains 200 mg of lidocaine. This counts toward the cumulative dose along with sprays, gels, and nerve blocks.

questions.stem: A nebulizer contains 8 mL of 4% lidocaine. What total lidocaine dose is being delivered?
questions.explanation: A 4% solution contains 40 mg/mL, so 8 mL contains 320 mg of lidocaine, though only part of a nebulized dose is absorbed. Many clinicians still count the full dose toward the maximum to stay safe.

questions.stem: A patient receives 8 mL of 4% lidocaine plus 2 mL of 2% lidocaine for each bilateral SLN block. What is the total dose?
questions.explanation: The nebulizer gives 8 mL of 4% lidocaine, or 320 mg, and two superior laryngeal blocks of 2 mL of 2% lidocaine each add 80 mg, for a total of 400 mg. This exceeds 4.5 mg/kg for a 70-kg patient, so dosing should be reviewed.

questions.stem: A patient with an unstable cervical spine requires intubation while minimizing neck movement and preserving neurologic assessment. Which technique is best?
questions.explanation: With an unstable cervical spine, awake flexible scope intubation with topical anesthesia avoids neck movement and allows a neurologic check after intubation and positioning. Video laryngoscopy with manual in-line stabilization is an alternative in urgent situations.

questions.stem: A patient with a large laryngeal tumor and stridor is at risk of losing the airway after induction. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Awake intubation or surgical airway preparation
Rapid sequence induction with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: A large laryngeal tumor with stridor suggests critical airway narrowing that may become complete after induction and loss of airway tone. Preserving spontaneous ventilation during an awake airway technique while preparing rescue access avoids committing to apnea before the airway is secured.

questions.stem: After induction, bag-mask ventilation remains impossible despite repositioning, OPA, and a two-hand seal while SpO2 falls. What should be done next?
options: Attempt intubation with a Mac blade
Give succinylcholine and retry the mask
questions.explanation: When bag-mask ventilation fails despite repositioning, an oral airway, and a two-hand technique, the next step is a supraglottic airway to restore oxygenation. Repeated laryngoscopy delays oxygenation, and paralysis may help if laryngospasm is suspected but does not replace the SGA step in the algorithm.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation and SGA rescue have failed, intubation is unsuccessful, and SpO2 is 70%. What is the next step?
options: Give sugammadex and wait to wake
questions.explanation: When mask ventilation, SGA rescue, and intubation have all failed with severe hypoxemia, the patient is in a CICO situation and needs emergency front-of-neck access. Another laryngoscopy or blind attempt wastes time, and waiting for recovery after sugammadex is too slow at an SpO2 of 70%.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy yields a Cormack-Lehane III view. Which next maneuver best improves the chance of successful intubation without repeated blind attempts?
options: Repeat DL with the same blade
Use a bougie or BURP, or switch to VL
Blind tube passage under the epiglottis
Wake the patient after one look
questions.explanation: With a grade III view, a bougie, external laryngeal manipulation such as BURP, or switching to a videolaryngoscope changes the approach and improves success while oxygenation is maintained. Repeating the same attempt rarely works, blind passage risks trauma, and waking is premature when ventilation is adequate.

questions.stem: A Cormack-Lehane IIb view shows only the posterior glottis. Which adjunct is most likely to facilitate tracheal tube placement?
questions.explanation: A bougie can be passed under the epiglottis and through the posterior glottis when only part of the glottis is visible, then the tube is railroaded over it. Lighted stylets are blind devices, Magill forceps guide a tube already seen in the pharynx, and a smaller tube does not solve the angle problem.

questions.stem: After intubation of a 165-cm woman, the tube is at 25 cm at the incisors and left breath sounds are faint. What depth is typical for her?
questions.explanation: A depth of about 21 cm at the upper incisors in women and 23 cm in men usually places the tip in the mid-trachea. At 25 cm with faint left breath sounds, the tube is likely in the right mainstem and should be withdrawn to about 21 cm with breath sounds rechecked. At 17 cm the cuff may sit at the cords.
